### 4.11 — High-Performance Computing

High-performance computing studies how to solve demanding computational problems within limits on time, memory, energy, and cost. The work may use one carefully optimized node or a large cluster. The goal is a useful result at the required accuracy, not simply keeping the largest number of processors busy.

Begin with three questions: which parts of the computation can proceed independently, where the data must move, and how the numerical method affects accuracy and work. A simulation divided across machines needs both local computation and communication at partition boundaries. More machines can reduce local work while increasing coordination and data-transfer costs.

This section connects architecture (§4.1) to linear algebra (§2.3), calculus (§2.4), and scientific computing (§6.5). Parallel algorithms, performance measurement, and numerical analysis explain how a mathematical method becomes an effective implementation.

*Prerequisites: Computer organization and architecture (§4.1), linear algebra (§2.3), and basic floating-point arithmetic. Numerical analysis becomes increasingly important when evaluating scientific results.*

#### From Ballistic Tables to Exascale: The Architecture of Scale

Large numerical projects existed before electronic computers. Teams of human computers divided calculations, followed procedures, and checked results. ENIAC was built to accelerate work including ballistic-table calculation; Haigh and Ceruzzi's account also emphasizes the people who organized and programmed such work. Faster arithmetic changed what was feasible, but useful computation still depended on decomposing the problem, supplying data, and validating the result.

The architecture of parallel computing developed through successive hardware generations, each with its own programming model and its own characteristic bottlenecks. Michael Flynn's 1966 taxonomy — SISD, SIMD, MISD, MIMD — classified the space of possible parallel computer architectures. SIMD (Single Instruction Multiple Data) machines apply the same instruction to multiple data elements simultaneously, which fits vector processing and graphics. MIMD (Multiple Instruction Multiple Data) machines allow independent instruction streams on multiple processors, which fits general parallel computation. This classification, though simple, organized the diversity of parallel hardware and is still used in reasoning about modern processors, which combine SIMD vector units with MIMD multi-core execution.

The Cray-1, first delivered in 1976, used vector registers and pipelined functional units to process sequences of elements efficiently. A vector register could hold 64 elements, but a vector instruction did not perform all 64 element operations simultaneously in one cycle. After pipeline startup, successive elements could move through the unit at a high rate. Regular operations and an adequate supply of data were central to obtaining that throughput.

Parallel machines explored both arrays of simple processing elements and systems with independently executing processors. They did not all use the same commodity components or programming model. MPI, standardized in 1994, provided a common interface for communication among processes, including point-to-point messages and collective operations. Portable interfaces reduced dependence on vendor-specific libraries, while performance still depended on decomposition, implementation, and interconnect.

The Beowulf project at NASA Goddard in 1994 demonstrated useful parallel scientific computing with commodity computers and networking. Clusters made some workloads affordable to more research groups. Commodity parts did not remove communication costs, software effort, or operating costs; the benefit depended on matching the application to the available cluster.

Graphics processors supplied increasing arithmetic throughput and memory bandwidth for suitable parallel work. Early general-purpose GPU computation adapted graphics interfaces; CUDA, released in 2007, exposed a more direct programming model. Scientific applications could use GPUs when their kernels supplied enough parallel work and suitable data access. Host-device transfer, irregular computation, and limited device memory remained engineering constraints.

Roadrunner in 2008 and Frontier in 2022 marked petaflop and exaflop milestones on the High Performance LINPACK benchmark. An exaflop is 10^18 floating-point operations per second. A benchmark result applies to its workload and precision; it is not the speed of every scientific application. Large systems also need effective interconnects, storage, scheduling, power, cooling, and recovery to turn arithmetic capacity into usable results.

Machine-learning training shares many HPC concerns: partitioning work, exchanging gradients or activations, fitting state into memory, and choosing numerical precision. Data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism divide different parts of that work. Skills transfer between scientific and ML workloads, but their communication patterns, accuracy criteria, and failure-recovery requirements still need separate analysis. Accelerator product names are less useful as a foundation than these recurring constraints.

#### Parallelism, Data Movement, and Hardware at Scale

Use a model to identify a possible limit, then measure whether the implementation approaches it. Separate fixed-workload speedup, larger-problem capacity, communication costs, and numerical accuracy.

#### Extracting and Managing Parallelism

Parallel decomposition assigns work while respecting dependencies. Amdahl's law models a fixed job whose serial fraction is `s`: ideal speedup on `p` processors is `1 / (s + (1-s)/p)`. With `s = 0.1` and eight processors, speedup is about 4.71; with infinitely many, it is at most ten. Communication and imbalance can make actual speedup lower. The serial fraction and ideal division are assumptions of the model, not quantities fixed for every input size.

Strong scaling keeps the problem fixed while adding processors. Weak scaling grows the problem with processor count, commonly keeping work per processor approximately fixed. Gustafson's scaled-workload perspective asks how much more work can be completed in a similar time. It addresses a different question from accelerating one fixed job and does not repeal Amdahl's limit.

In the work-span model, work `W` is total operation cost and span `S` is the longest dependency chain. With `p` ideal processors, execution time is at least `max(W/p, S)`, and available parallelism is bounded by `W/S`. Reducing span may require additional work or storage. For example, a tree reduction has logarithmic dependency depth, unlike a sequential accumulator's linear chain, while still performing a linear number of additions.

OpenMP commonly expresses shared-memory parallel work; MPI supplies process communication, collectives, and other facilities; GPU models expose groups of many device threads. Separate MPI address spaces remove some shared-variable hazards, but do not eliminate races in threaded code, communication buffers, or shared-memory and remote-memory operations. Matching messages, completing nonblocking operations before reusing buffers, and agreeing on collective participation are correctness requirements.

A two-dimensional grid simulation illustrates the scaling cost. If each square partition has side length `n`, its local work can grow like `n²`, while exchanging a one-cell boundary grows like `n`. Dividing a fixed grid into more, smaller partitions increases boundary traffic relative to local work. Overlapping communication with independent interior computation can help, but only when dependencies and the implementation permit it.

#### Data Movement and Performance Limits

Data movement can limit performance through latency, bandwidth, or energy cost. A chain of dependent loads may be latency-limited; many independent transfers may saturate bandwidth. Comparing the latency of one arithmetic instruction with one memory access does not by itself predict the throughput of a whole kernel, because operations can overlap.

The Roofline model connects arithmetic intensity `I`—operations per byte moved across a specified memory boundary—to bandwidth `B` and arithmetic capacity `F`. Its basic ceiling is `performance ≤ min(F, B×I)`. For an illustrative device with `F = 100 GFLOP/s`, `B = 50 GB/s`, and `I = 0.25 FLOP/byte`, the bandwidth ceiling is 12.5 GFLOP/s. Increasing arithmetic capacity alone does not raise that ceiling. Actual performance may be lower because of latency, dependencies, instruction mix, or poor utilization.

Specify the precision and memory level when using this model. Traffic between registers and cache is different from traffic between device memory and a host. Raising arithmetic intensity by eliminating unnecessary transfers can help; merely adding useless arithmetic can raise the ratio without reducing time to solution. Compare useful elapsed time as well as FLOP/s.

Matrix tiling reuses blocks in fast storage before replacing them. The arithmetic can remain the same while transfers to slower storage decrease. Distributed algorithms such as Cannon's and SUMMA organize matrix partitions and communication; some replication-based algorithms spend extra memory to reduce communication. The tradeoff is among computation, movement, capacity, and synchronization, not a universal rule that every faster method performs more arithmetic.

#### Floating-Point and Numerical Correctness

Floating-point arithmetic approximates real arithmetic with finite precision and range. Under ordinary binary64 rounding, `(1e16 + (-1e16)) + 1` gives 1, while `1e16 + ((-1e16) + 1)` gives 0. The inner addition in the second expression rounds away the unit difference. Changing a parallel reduction's order can therefore change its result without a race or a compiler bug.

Conditioning describes the problem: how much can the exact answer change when the input changes slightly? Stability describes the algorithm: how do its rounding errors affect the answer? A backward-stable method returns the exact answer to a nearby input problem; an ill-conditioned problem can still turn that small input perturbation into a large forward error. Pivoting concerns the numerical behavior of elimination, not an improvement to the original problem's condition number.

A deterministic reduction order can improve reproducibility, while pairwise or compensated summation can improve accuracy under appropriate assumptions. These are different goals: a reproducible answer can still be inaccurate, and compensated summation alone does not guarantee identical bits across every order or platform. State whether the requirement is a numerical tolerance, stable convergence, or bit-for-bit identity.

Mixed precision uses different representations for different stages. Lower precision can reduce storage and increase throughput; higher-precision accumulation or iterative refinement can recover accuracy for suitable problems. Validate the method's convergence and error, not just whether a benchmark runs faster. Compare against known solutions, residuals, refinement studies, or an independently computed reference as appropriate to the problem.

#### What Studying This Changes

Measure time to a validated result. First establish the input, algorithm, precision, and baseline; then compare processor counts and report both speedup and resource cost. A faster kernel may leave total runtime unchanged if communication, loading, or checkpointing dominates.

A useful exercise is to compare a sequential sum with a parallel tree reduction, then vary the input magnitudes. Observe dependency depth, elapsed time, and numerical differences separately. For a grid simulation, keep the grid fixed while adding workers, then enlarge the grid with the worker count. The two experiments make strong and weak scaling concrete.

These habits transfer beyond supercomputers. Data layout, bounded dependencies, appropriate precision, and a clear performance hypothesis also improve ordinary numerical programs. Use added hardware only when the computation can make useful use of it.

## Chapter 5 — Artificial Intelligence

### 5.1 — Classical AI and Symbolic Approaches

Classical AI studies methods for representing a problem explicitly and using that representation to search, infer, or plan. A route planner describes locations, permitted moves, and costs; a theorem prover describes statements and inference rules; a scheduling system describes assignments and constraints. The useful starting question is: what must the system represent to choose a justified next step?

**Symbolic** describes representations with explicit structure and interpretation, such as a logical formula or an action with preconditions. It does not mean that all knowledge must be entered by hand or that numbers and learning are excluded. A search procedure can use a learned heuristic; a robot can combine learned perception with an explicit planner. Representation, inference, learning, and action are different design choices that can be combined.

This section develops state spaces, heuristics, knowledge bases, constraints, and plans. These concepts connect AI to algorithms (§2.6), logic (§3.1), and formal methods (§3.6). They help explain both successful systems and failures caused by leaving a relevant distinction out of the model.

*Prerequisites: Basic graph algorithms (§2.6), sets and relations (§2.2), and propositional logic (§3.1). Learn `A*`, resolution, and planning here; they are not prerequisites for starting this section.*

#### From the Founding Optimism to the Knowledge Representation Crisis

The 1956 Dartmouth project helped establish AI as a named research field. Its 1955 proposal was written by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon. The participants brought different interests, including neural networks, learning, language, and symbolic problem solving. Nilsson's history makes this diversity visible: AI did not begin as one unified method later replaced by learning.

Newell, Shaw, and Simon's Logic Theorist demonstrated heuristic theorem proving. Their later General Problem Solver used means–ends analysis: compare the current and desired situations, then select operations that reduce a difference, introducing subgoals when necessary. The lasting contribution was to express problem solving as a search over representations and operators. Choosing those representations remained substantial work.

SRI's Shakey robot made that work concrete. A mobile robot needed to turn observations into a world model, choose routes around obstacles, plan actions, and execute them through imperfect hardware. `A*` emerged from work on heuristic path search; STRIPS represented actions through preconditions and changes to facts. Perception, planning, and control had to agree about what a state and an action meant. A correct plan for an inaccurate map could still fail during execution.

Winograd's SHRDLU showed how language processing, reasoning, and action could cooperate in a restricted blocks world. Its small domain supplied explicit objects, relations, and possible actions. Extending such a system required additional representations and procedures; a convincing demonstration in a controlled world did not establish open-domain language understanding. The lesson concerns the work hidden in specifying a domain, rather than a proof that symbolic methods cannot scale.

Expert systems made domain knowledge more explicit. DENDRAL used chemical knowledge to constrain the search for molecular structures; MYCIN explored rule-based reasoning about infections and treatment recommendations. XCON configured computer orders at Digital Equipment Corporation. These projects showed that useful expertise could be encoded, but acquiring, validating, and maintaining it was expensive. MYCIN's research evaluations did not establish the effectiveness of routine clinical deployment. Success on a bounded task and integration into an institution were separate achievements.

The ALPAC report of 1966 and the Lighthill report of 1973 challenged particular programs, expectations, and funding priorities. Later commercial disappointment, the cost of maintaining expert systems, and competition from general-purpose workstations contributed to another contraction. The term “AI winter” summarizes changes in support; it should not imply that all research stopped or that one theorem caused every setback. Nilsson documents continued work and uneven effects across projects.

Different responses addressed different limitations. Cyc pursued explicit commonsense knowledge. Nonmonotonic reasoning studied conclusions that may need revision when new facts arrive. Bayesian networks represented joint probability distributions through conditional structure, making dependence assumptions and uncertain inference explicit. They did not make missing knowledge disappear or make all inference efficient. A probabilistic dependency also does not by itself establish a causal relation.

SAT solving illustrates progress within a difficult worst-case problem. Clause learning records consequences of conflicts so later search can avoid related failures. Its practical success depends on instance structure and implementation, without removing NP-completeness. SMT adds theories such as arithmetic and bit vectors. These methods connect AI research with verification and constraint solving across computer science.

AlphaGo combined policy and value networks with Monte Carlo tree search, using supervised learning and self-play in its development. The networks helped allocate search effort and evaluate positions; search used the game's explicit rules to explore consequences. This combination illustrates how learned estimates and explicit computation can cooperate. Generating a language-model reasoning trace is a different mechanism and should be assessed on its own evidence, rather than assumed to implement the same search algorithm.

#### Search, Knowledge, Reasoning, and Planning

#### Search: States, Costs, and Heuristics

A search problem specifies states, an initial state, available actions, transition rules, a goal test, and a cost. State design matters: in a maze with locked doors, position alone is insufficient if carrying a key changes which moves are possible. Treating “same position, with key” and “same position, without key” as identical can discard the only solution.

`A*` orders candidates by `f(n) = g(n) + h(n)`: the cost of the best discovered route to a state plus an estimate of the remaining cost. On a four-neighbor grid with unit move costs, Manhattan distance from `(0,0)` to `(3,2)` is 5. Obstacles may require a longer route, but cannot make fewer than five moves sufficient, so the estimate is admissible. A consistent heuristic also satisfies `h(u) ≤ c(u,v) + h(v)` for every edge, with zero at a goal. On a finite graph with nonnegative costs, this condition supports the usual `A*` implementation that closes states after expansion. With an admissible but inconsistent heuristic, improved routes may require reopening states. The [Berkeley search project](https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs188/sp21/project1/) makes these conditions part of implementing the algorithm.

Setting `h = 0` gives uniform-cost search. Better justified lower bounds can reduce expansions, but `A*` does not universally examine the fewest nodes of every possible algorithm. Pattern databases obtain lower bounds by solving abstractions of a problem. The abstraction and how bounds are combined must preserve the lower-bound property. Heuristic quality, memory use, and the cost of computing the heuristic all matter.

Minimax models an adversary selecting replies; alpha–beta pruning avoids branches that cannot change the fixed-depth minimax result. Good move ordering can save enough work to search deeper within a budget. Monte Carlo tree search instead uses repeated sampling and value estimates to allocate simulations among moves. Its evaluations may come from rollouts or learned models, and finite-budget estimates are not exact minimax guarantees.

#### Knowledge Representation: The Problem of Encoding What You Know

A representation specifies which distinctions the system can express. First-order logic represents objects, relations, functions, and quantified claims. Description logics restrict forms of description to support particular reasoning tasks. A knowledge graph records entities and relationships, but the graph alone does not determine how missing facts, conflicting sources, or inference should be handled. RDF graphs can be queried with SPARQL; other graph models use other query languages.

Missing information illustrates a consequential choice. If a database contains no record that a room is occupied, does that mean it is empty, or that occupancy is unknown? A closed-world convention treats specified missing facts as false; an open-world convention leaves them unknown. Neither convention is universally right. A booking system and an incomplete scientific knowledge base may need different assumptions.

The frame problem asks how to express what persists after an action without listing a separate non-change statement for every unrelated fact. Moving a box changes its location but normally leaves its color unchanged. STRIPS-style add/delete lists and logical successor-state axioms provide compact treatments under stated assumptions. They do not solve every problem of identifying relevant effects, exceptions, or unforeseen events. The distinction is between representing persistence within a model and knowing whether the model includes the effects that matter.

Uncertain evidence calls for additional machinery. A Bayesian network factors a joint distribution using conditional probabilities; a logical rule specifies an implication under its interpretation. A rule's confidence score is not automatically a calibrated probability. Learning facts, estimating probabilities, and checking logical consequences can all be parts of one knowledge system.

#### Automated Reasoning and Planning

Resolution proves consequences by refutation: combine the premises with the negation of the proposed conclusion, transform them appropriately into clauses, and search for a contradiction. First-order resolution with unification is refutation complete under a suitable search strategy. This does not provide a terminating decision procedure for every first-order input. Prolog's clause selection and depth-first execution can also fail to terminate even when another search order would find an answer.

SAT asks for a satisfying assignment to a propositional formula. SMT adds a theory specifying the meaning of operations on domains such as integers, arrays, or bit vectors. A returned assignment must be interpreted back in the application model. Unsatisfiability can reveal conflicting requirements; it can also reveal an encoding mistake. A timeout or “unknown” answer establishes neither satisfiability nor impossibility.

Classical planning describes actions through preconditions and effects. Suppose `Move(A,B)` requires `At(A)` and `Clear(B)`, adds `At(B)`, and deletes `At(A)`. Other facts persist under the chosen action model. A plan is a sequence whose successive states satisfy each action's preconditions and whose final state meets the goal. If obtaining a key is necessary to open a door, the planner must establish that precondition before using the doorway.

STRIPS made this representation explicit; PDDL supports describing planning domains and problems, with extensions for additional features. A bounded planning problem can also be encoded as SAT by representing states and actions at each step. Failure to find a plan of length at most ten does not establish that no longer plan exists. During execution, sensing, monitoring, and replanning address discrepancies between predicted and observed states. Planning and acting are therefore connected but distinct tasks.

#### What Studying This Changes

You should be able to separate a real task from its search or reasoning model. State which information determines available actions, which facts are assumed, what counts as a solution, and whether the objective asks for any solution or an optimal one. A model can be internally consistent while omitting a practical requirement.

Implement a small maze search with both `h = 0` and Manhattan distance. Check path cost against a reference solver and record expanded states and peak frontier size. Then add keys and doors. Changing the state from a position to a position plus inventory demonstrates why representation can matter more than changing the search routine.

Connect these ideas to other methods: a learned model may supply a heuristic, a solver may check a generated candidate, and a planner may organize tool calls. Determine what each component guarantees and how failures are detected at their interfaces. Historical examples help identify these recurring design problems without predicting that every new approach must repeat the same outcome.

#### Resources

**Books and Texts**

Use Russell and Norvig's **Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach** as the main reference for search, logic, planning, and probabilistic reasoning. Work through a search problem and a small planning domain before moving to specialized texts. Nilsson's **The Quest for Artificial Intelligence** supplies historical context: its accounts of Shakey and expert systems show which practical problems motivated these methods.

Choose further reading by the question you need to answer. Pearl's **Heuristics** develops search; Brachman and Levesque explain representation and inference; Ghallab, Nau, and Traverso connect planning models to action. Kroening and Strichman's **Decision Procedures** introduces SAT and SMT. Pearl's books on probabilistic reasoning and causality address different questions: predicting from observations and reasoning about interventions require different assumptions. Read Dreyfus and Marcus/Davis as arguments to assess against examples, rather than as proofs that a whole approach must fail.

#### Traps

| Trap | Why it misleads | Better response |
|---|---|---|
| Treating classical AI as only historical | Search, constraints, and explicit action models solve identifiable engineering tasks. | Model a scheduling or navigation task, then compare a solver with a simple baseline. |
| Treating the frame problem as either trivial or universally unsolved | Persistence has compact formal treatments, while relevance and unforeseen effects require additional modeling. | State the action model and check which facts persist and which effects it omits. |
| Inferring practical impossibility from NP-completeness | Worst-case hardness does not describe every structured or bounded instance. | Inspect the instance family, available heuristics, and measured search cost. |
| Making neural and symbolic methods mutually exclusive | Learning an estimate and searching with it are compatible operations. | Identify representation, learning, inference, and checking as separate design choices. |
| Using a plausible heuristic without checking its guarantee | Overestimation or inconsistent state handling can invalidate an optimality claim. | Prove the required lower-bound or consistency property and test duplicate-state handling. |

### 5.2 — Machine Learning Foundations

Machine learning constructs or adapts a model using data. The model may predict a label, estimate a probability, discover structure, generate an example, or choose an action. Learning still requires a program and design decisions: what data is available, which models are considered, what objective is optimized, and how success will be measured.

In supervised learning, examples include target outputs. In unsupervised learning, the learner seeks structure without those task labels. Self-supervised learning creates prediction targets from the data itself, such as a missing word or the next token. Reinforcement learning (§5.4) concerns decisions and reward over time. These distinctions describe the learning signal; they do not determine one particular architecture.

The central separation is between **fitting the observed data** and **performing the intended task on new cases**. A classifier can learn which camera photographed an object instead of the object's relevant properties. Excellent training accuracy would then measure success at exploiting the dataset, without establishing success at the intended task. This section develops generalization, inductive bias, optimization, and evaluation as connected questions.

*Prerequisites: Vectors and matrices (§2.3), probability and expectations (§2.5), and derivatives (§2.4). Begin with linear models and small datasets; advanced matrix calculus and learning-theory proofs can follow as needed.*

#### From Learning Programs to Statistical Learning

Learning was part of AI from its early years. Arthur Samuel's checkers work combined search with methods for improving position evaluation from experience. Rosenblatt's perceptron supplied a trainable linear decision rule. These projects addressed a practical difficulty: specifying every useful decision by hand becomes expensive, while examples or interaction can supply information about which decisions work.

The perceptron convergence theorem applies to linearly separable training data. XOR supplies a small limitation of a linear threshold classifier: the positive points `(0,1)` and `(1,0)` cannot be separated by one straight boundary from `(0,0)` and `(1,1)`. This is a representational limitation of that model, not a theorem that multilayer networks cannot learn. Minsky and Papert's analysis influenced debate, while compute, funding, algorithms, and competing approaches also shaped subsequent research.

Statistical learning theory connected prediction to assumptions about sampling and model classes. Vapnik and Chervonenkis studied conditions under which empirical frequencies uniformly approximate probabilities over a class. Valiant's 1984 PAC framework made accuracy and confidence explicit and connected learning to computational efficiency. “Enough examples” could now be a mathematical question, although its answer depended on the learning setup.

Backpropagation made gradient calculation in multilayer models practical and became widely influential after Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams's 1986 work. It has a longer history in differentiation and learning research. The important distinction is between computing a gradient and having a training procedure that succeeds: the objective, initialization, data, architecture, and optimization schedule still matter.

Kernel methods offered nonlinear prediction through inner products in a feature space. A support vector machine balances separation and margin, with soft-margin versions allowing violations. A kernel evaluates a feature-space inner product without necessarily constructing the feature vectors. Computing a Gaussian kernel still requires comparing the input vectors; the method does not make high-dimensional computation or storing many pairwise comparisons free.

Decision trees, bagging, random forests, and boosting developed complementary ways to combine predictors. Bagging can reduce instability by averaging models fitted to resampled data. Boosting adds models to improve a chosen objective, often by fitting information from the remaining errors or gradients. These methods remain useful alternatives to neural networks; their value should be assessed for the actual data and constraints rather than asserted as a universal ranking.

Larger datasets, improved training methods, and parallel hardware expanded what neural networks could learn. Their success also exposed limits of simple rules based only on parameter count. Double-descent experiments showed that test error can rise near interpolation and fall again as capacity increases. This does not falsify the bias–variance identity or guarantee that larger models always improve. It shows why the algorithm, regularization, data distribution, and way capacity is varied belong in the explanation.

#### Generalization, Inductive Bias, Optimization, and Evaluation

#### Generalization: The Central Problem

Let `R(f)` be a predictor's expected loss under the target distribution, and `R̂(f)` its average loss on the training sample. Training can reduce the second without reducing the first. The generalization gap compares them, while the total error also depends on the quality of the model class, optimization, label noise, and the target distribution itself. Low training error is one observation, not a complete diagnosis.

A simple PAC bound shows how assumptions do work. Suppose binary labels are noise-free, the correct rule belongs to a finite class `H`, and examples are drawn independently from the same distribution used for evaluation. A learner choosing a rule consistent with all training labels has error at most `ε`, with probability at least `1−δ`, for `0 < ε, δ < 1` once `m ≥ (ln|H| + ln(1/δ))/ε`. Intuitively, a rule with error greater than `ε` is unlikely to survive many independent tests; accounting for every candidate introduces the class-size term. The bound does not apply unchanged to noisy labels, dependent samples, or arbitrary distribution shift.

VC dimension extends this capacity analysis beyond finite classes by asking how many points a class can label in every possible way. Affine half-plane classifiers in two dimensions have VC dimension 3. A capacity measure is not simply the number of stored parameters, and a loose worst-case bound does not predict a particular network's test error. Margin, norm, stability, and PAC-Bayes analyses examine other properties of learners and solutions.

For squared loss at a fixed input, the bias–variance decomposition separates squared bias of the average predictor, variation between predictors trained on different samples, and conditional outcome noise. It is an identity under the relevant expectations. It does not require that variance grow monotonically with every measure of model size. Regularization and the optimization algorithm can change which solution is selected even when many models fit the sample perfectly.

#### Inductive Bias: Assumptions Behind Prediction

Inductive bias is a learner's preference among explanations compatible with the observed data. With only two examples, `f(0)=0` and `f(1)=1`, both `f(x)=x` and `f(x)=x²` fit perfectly, but predict different values at `x=2`. More generally, finite observations leave many possible rules. Assumptions about smoothness, symmetry, sparsity, or simplicity make prediction beyond those observations possible.

Bias enters through representation, model class, loss, regularization, optimization, and data collection. A linear model is linear in its chosen features; adding `x²` as a feature makes nonlinear dependence on the original input possible. Convolution shares a local computation across positions, supporting translation equivariance under appropriate boundary and stride conditions. It does not make every complete CNN translation-invariant. Attention supplies content-dependent interactions, whose allowed pattern also depends on masking and positional information.

Regularization changes which fits are preferred. In ridge regression, minimizing squared error plus `λ‖w‖²` penalizes large coefficients; the effect depends on feature scaling. Rescaling one feature changes the coefficient needed to express the same predictor and thus its penalty. Preprocessing and regularization are therefore connected modeling choices. Learned representations reduce some manual feature work, while leaving data construction and architecture choices consequential.

#### Optimization: Fitting the Training Objective

Optimization adjusts a model to reduce a specified objective. For prediction `ŷ = wx` and loss `L = ½(wx−y)²`, the gradient is `(wx−y)x`. At `x=2`, `y=4`, and `w=1`, the loss is 2 and the gradient is −4. A gradient-descent step with learning rate `0.1` gives `w=1.4`, reducing this example's loss to `0.72`. The calculation explains the update; it supplies no evidence yet about performance on new inputs.

Full-batch gradient descent uses the entire training set for each gradient. Minibatch SGD estimates that gradient using sampled examples, reducing the cost per update. Under uniform sampling its estimate is unbiased for the finite-sample objective, but updates have variance. Batch size, learning rate, momentum, and sampling affect both computation and the optimization path. Adam rescales updates using estimates of gradient moments; it is not automatically preferable for every objective or workload.

Convergence results require assumptions about the objective, gradient estimates, and step sizes. Convexity can support guarantees about global optima; smooth nonconvex analyses often instead bound a measure of stationarity. Neither statement guarantees that a finite training run has reached the desired solution. A zero gradient may occur at a saddle, and good training loss does not establish generalization.

Optimization also selects among solutions. Particular linear-model settings admit precise results about implicit bias toward a norm or margin; those results do not provide one universal explanation of deep learning. Check learning curves, gradient magnitudes, parameter updates, and sensitivity to seeds. A small numerical gradient check is useful when implementing derivatives; it does not validate the dataset or the learning objective.

#### Evaluation: Measuring Performance on New Data

Design the split around the intended prediction. To predict future observations, use a temporal separation; to generalize to new users or devices, hold out those groups. Randomly splitting individual records can put nearly identical cases from the same source on both sides. Fit preprocessing, feature selection, and hyperparameter choices using training data and validation procedures, leaving the final test set outside those choices.

For a small dataset, cross-validation can help estimate performance and select settings; nested cross-validation separates model selection from its evaluation. Repeatedly using a test score to guide revisions makes that test part of development. Reusing the same fixed test solely for a declared report is a different activity, but adaptive comparisons still require accounting for selection. The important issue is how information from evaluation influences decisions.

Match metrics to errors that matter. If only ten of a thousand items are defective, always predicting “not defective” gives 99% accuracy while detecting none. Precision measures how many flagged cases are true positives; recall measures how many positives were found. Decision thresholds trade these quantities against each other, while calibration asks whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. A cost-sensitive decision may need different thresholds even when the probability model is unchanged.

Distinguish leakage from distribution shift. Leakage supplies information that should not be available during development or at prediction time; shift changes the relationship between evaluated and deployed data. Report uncertainty, group performance, relevant baselines, and failure cases. More data helps only insofar as its sampling and labels provide useful information for the target task.

#### What Studying This Changes

You should be able to describe a learning problem before choosing a library: the prediction time, available inputs, target population, learning signal, loss, and evaluation metric. These choices determine what a successful experiment would demonstrate.

Build a small baseline, inspect its mistakes, and change one justified aspect at a time. High training loss can reflect limited representation, optimization problems, noisy labels, or preprocessing errors. A large evaluation gap can reflect overfitting, sampling differences, or a broken evaluation pipeline. Use evidence to distinguish these explanations instead of treating one curve as a unique diagnosis.

Implement linear or logistic regression once, compare analytical gradients with numerical differences, and reproduce the result with a library. Then deliberately create a leaky split or fit preprocessing on the full dataset and observe the evaluation change. Understanding both the update rule and the evaluation procedure prepares you to judge later deep learning and language-model experiments.

### 5.3 — Deep Learning

Deep learning trains compositions of parameterized functions to construct useful representations and outputs. In an image classifier, early computations may detect local patterns and later computations combine information over larger regions. What is learned depends on the data and objective; a neatly labeled hierarchy of human concepts is not guaranteed.

Nonlinearity matters as much as depth. Several linear transformations with no intervening nonlinearity collapse into one matrix multiplication. Nonlinear layers expand the functions that can be represented. Universal-approximation results for suitable single-hidden-layer networks concern approximation under specified assumptions, not exact computation of every function, efficient representation, or successful learning from finite data. Expressibility, trainability, and generalization are separate questions.

Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute parameter gradients. An optimizer uses those gradients to update parameters. Keeping these operations separate helps diagnose whether a problem comes from the model, derivative calculation, update rule, data, or evaluation. This section adds architectural and training mechanisms to the learning framework in §5.2.

*Prerequisites: Small-model training and evaluation (§5.2), matrix operations (§2.3), and the chain rule (§2.4). Begin with a small multilayer network before studying large architectures.*

#### From Perceptrons to Transformers: The Empirical Development of a Discipline

Early neural-network research investigated how adjustable connections could support recognition and learning. Rosenblatt's perceptron made a linear decision rule trainable from examples. Its limitations motivated richer representations; they did not settle the capabilities of all multilayer networks. Work continued through periods of reduced attention, including research on differentiation, associative memory, and recurrent systems.

Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams's 1986 work helped establish backpropagation as a practical method for learning intermediate representations. The chain rule supplied an efficient way to assign derivatives to many parameters. It did not remove problems caused by saturation, ill-conditioned optimization, limited data, or expensive computation.

Convolutional networks developed from ideas about local receptive fields and shared computations. LeCun and collaborators demonstrated gradient-based learning for handwritten character and document recognition. By the 1990s, these methods had practical applications. Locality and weight sharing reduced the number of independent parameters needed to process an image; their usefulness came from matching a problem's structure, not from using biologically suggestive terminology.

Recurrent networks reused a state update over time. Long dependencies exposed vanishing and exploding gradients, and LSTM introduced a memory path with gates controlling retention and updates. Kernel methods and other statistical techniques developed alongside this work. The history contains overlapping approaches with different strengths, rather than a complete replacement of one school by another.

Layer-wise pretraining attracted renewed attention in the 2000s. The subsequent expansion of deep learning depended on several changes together: datasets, GPUs, nonlinearities, initialization, regularization, software, and experimental practice. AlexNet's 2012 ImageNet result demonstrated the effectiveness of one such combination. ImageNet as a collection and the particular classification challenge's training subset should not be treated as the same dataset size.

Architectures and objectives then diversified. Residual connections made very deep networks easier to optimize; normalization changed activation scales and training behavior. Sequence-to-sequence models and attention improved handling of variable-length inputs and outputs. GANs trained a generator against a discriminator, while variational autoencoders used a latent-variable objective with approximate inference. These are different learning formulations, not merely larger versions of a classifier.

The 2017 transformer used attention in place of recurrence for sequence modeling. During training, known tokens at many positions can be processed in parallel while masks enforce permitted information flow. Autoregressive generation still ordinarily produces successive tokens sequentially. BERT and GPT developed different pretraining objectives and adaptation methods on transformer architectures; transfer learning itself predates both.

Empirical scaling studies measured how loss changes with parameters, training data, and compute. They made resource allocation a quantitative research question. Later work investigated alternatives such as state-space sequence models, sparse mixtures of experts, and diffusion-based generation. Their tradeoffs include memory, communication, latency, data requirements, and which computations the objective requires. No single architecture or scale law explains every successful learning system.

#### Architectures, Training, and What Scale Changes

#### Architecture as Inductive Bias

Architecture determines which computations share parameters and how information can move. A convolution applies the same filter at multiple positions. Under suitable stride and boundary conditions, translating the input translates the feature map: **equivariance**. **Invariance** would mean leaving the output unchanged. Pooling, padding, downsampling, and the final readout affect which property the complete model has. For digit classification, some positional changes should preserve the label; for locating an object, position must remain recoverable.

Recurrent models summarize preceding inputs in a state, repeatedly applying an update such as `hₜ = F(hₜ₋₁, xₜ)`. LSTM and GRU gates regulate what is retained or replaced. The summary has finite capacity, and ordinary recurrence creates dependencies between time steps that limit training parallelism. The advantage is a state that can be updated as observations arrive.

Attention forms content-dependent weighted combinations. Queries and keys determine weights; values carry the information being combined. Dense self-attention compares pairs of positions, with quadratic pairwise work in sequence length for fixed feature dimensions. Causal or sparse masks restrict available connections. Positional information is necessary when order matters; attention connectivity alone does not specify order.

Graph neural networks aggregate information along edges, using shared operations and often order-independent aggregation over neighbors. This fits problems where relationships are part of the input. The graph definition and aggregation rule determine which distinctions the model can make; message passing does not automatically distinguish every pair of different graphs.

Generative architectures add different objectives. An autoregressive model predicts successive parts; a diffusion model learns to reverse a specified corruption process; a variational autoencoder learns a latent-variable model through a tractable training bound. Select architecture and objective together, then compare data requirements, quality, sampling cost, and the forms of conditioning the task needs.

#### Training at Depth: Gradient Flow and Normalization

Backpropagation multiplies local derivatives along paths and adds contributions from different paths. A simplified chain with derivative `0.5` at each of twenty stages gives `0.5²⁰ ≈ 0.000000954`; with derivative `1.5`, the product is about 3325. These scalar examples explain vanishing and exploding gradients. Real networks involve Jacobians, whose directions and interactions matter as well as their magnitudes.

A residual block computes `y = x + F(x)`, so its Jacobian is `I + J_F(x)`. The identity term provides a path that does not pass through every derivative inside `F`. It helps optimization without guaranteeing that every gradient remains well-scaled. Initialization, activation functions, normalization, and depth still interact.

Normalization methods operate over different axes. Batch normalization uses batch statistics, often also aggregating spatial positions within each channel, and normally uses running statistics at inference. Layer normalization uses selected features within each example, commonly within one token representation. RMS normalization rescales by a root-mean-square statistic without subtracting the mean. These operations affect numerical scale and optimization; “removing internal covariate shift” is not a complete established explanation of all their benefits.

Initialization controls early signal and gradient scales. Glorot-style and He-style choices use layer widths and activation assumptions to choose parameter variance. Saturated activations, extreme scales, or an overly large learning rate can make an otherwise expressive network difficult to train. Diagnose the actual activations and gradients rather than treating one named initializer as a guarantee.

Weight decay also depends on the optimizer. With plain SGD, an L2 penalty produces a proportional shrinkage term under the corresponding convention. With adaptive preconditioning, adding that penalty to the gradient generally differs from directly shrinking parameters. AdamW separates weight decay from the adaptive gradient update. Record optimizer settings, schedules, precision, clipping, and normalization behavior when comparing training runs.

#### What Scale Changes: Emergent Capabilities and Scaling Laws

Scaling laws are empirical fits for specified model families, data, objectives, and training procedures. A common form separates an irreducible loss level from terms that decrease with parameters or training tokens. The exponents and useful range must be estimated; there is no universal “0.07 per decade” rule for model capability. Lower language-model loss is also not a direct measure of truthfulness, tool-use success, or every downstream task.

Kaplan and colleagues studied these relationships in 2020. Hoffmann and colleagues' [Chinchilla study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556) used a different experimental allocation to estimate how model size and token count should grow together under a fixed training-compute budget. Its recommendations concern that optimization problem. A deployment serving many requests may favor spending more training compute on a smaller model to reduce later inference cost. Data quality, repeated data, hardware efficiency, and post-training can change the practical allocation.

Apparent capability thresholds also depend on measurement. Suppose a toy task requires ten independent correct steps, each with success probability `p`. All-correct accuracy is `p¹⁰`: increasing per-step success from `0.8` to `0.9` increases full-task success from about `10.7%` to `34.9%`. The underlying improvement is smooth, yet the aggregate changes strongly; a small test may record no successes until the model improves. [Schaeffer and colleagues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.15004) showed how metric choices can produce apparent emergence in studied model families. This does not prove that all changes with scale are measurement artifacts.

Evaluate both intermediate performance and completed-task success, report uncertainty, and test extrapolations outside the fitted range. In-context learning has no universal parameter-count threshold. Small-model experiments can reveal mechanisms and reject bad designs, while quantitative predictions about a larger system still need validation. Neither smooth loss curves nor a sudden benchmark increase settles how a capability will behave in deployment.

#### What Studying This Changes

You should be able to trace a small network's forward computation, gradients, and parameter updates, and explain which architectural choices share information or parameters. Implementing a small CNN or attention layer is useful when accompanied by checks of dimensions, masks, and gradients.

Run controlled comparisons. To study a residual connection, compare otherwise similar models and record optimization behavior as well as final scores. To study data augmentation, specify which transformations should preserve the target and test whether they do. An ablation supports a claim within its training and evaluation setup; removing a component without retuning may mix that component's effect with a change in optimization conditions.

Learn to investigate failures through several measurements: training and validation loss, gradient norms, activation scales, data examples, throughput, and memory. A flat validation curve does not uniquely identify a cause. A useful experiment changes a suspected cause and tests a prediction about what should improve.

#### Traps

| Trap | Why it misleads | Better response |
|---|---|---|
| Equating framework fluency with understanding | Automatic differentiation hides bookkeeping, not the need to specify a valid computation. | Trace one forward and backward pass and check dimensions and gradients. |
| Choosing architecture by popularity | Parameter sharing and information flow may not match the task. | Identify relevant structure and compare a simpler model. |
| Reading a score gain as a mechanism explanation | Several changes in data, optimization, or evaluation can produce the gain. | Use controlled comparisons and examine alternative explanations. |
| Assuming scale guarantees a desired capability | Loss scaling, task metrics, and deployment success are different quantities. | Fit within a stated range and evaluate the capability directly. |
| Treating data work as secondary | Sampling, labels, duplicates, and transformations determine the learning signal. | Inspect data and document the construction of each split. |
| Treating theory as either a full prediction or irrelevant | Theorems explain particular models and assumptions, while experiments assess implementations. | Use theory to formulate a testable expectation and identify its conditions. |

### 5.4 — Reinforcement Learning

Reinforcement learning studies how to learn decisions from experience when actions affect later observations and rewards. The learner may collect that experience through interaction or use an existing dataset. It seeks a policy: a rule for choosing actions from the information available to the agent.

The distinctive difficulty is sequential feedback. An action can change both the eventual outcome and what the learner gets to observe next. Reward may arrive long after the relevant choice, so the agent must estimate long-term consequences, explore uncertain alternatives, and learn from incomplete feedback. Predicting a label and choosing an action are different tasks even when both use neural networks.

RL connects dynamic programming, optimal control, probability, and learning. A known environment model permits planning; an unknown model requires learning from data, possibly learning a model first and then planning with it. This distinction links the search methods in §5.1 to value functions and policy learning here.

*Prerequisites: Expectations and conditional probabilities (§2.5), basic optimization (§5.2), and dynamic programming (§2.6). Deep learning (§5.3) is needed for deep RL, but small tabular problems provide the clearest starting point.*

#### From Bellman's Equations to Language Model Alignment

RL grew from several traditions. Psychological studies examined learning through consequences; optimal control and Bellman's dynamic programming formalized sequential decision problems; early AI programs experimented with learning from play. Nilsson traces these overlapping contributions. There was no single clean progression from a completed theory to its later applications.

Bellman's value equations decompose a long-term objective into immediate reward and the value of a successor state. If transition probabilities and rewards are known, dynamic programming can use that model directly. The difficulty is often the number of states required to represent the problem, especially when several state variables vary independently.

Samuel's checkers program learned aspects of position evaluation while using search and domain-specific design. Sutton's temporal-difference work developed learning from the discrepancy between successive predictions: a prediction can be updated toward an observed reward plus a later estimate before the final outcome arrives. This bootstrapping offers a different bias–variance and data-use tradeoff from waiting for a completed return; it is not universally more accurate or efficient.

Watkins's Q-learning connected sampled transitions to learning optimal action values. Its tabular convergence results require conditions such as adequate visits to state–action pairs and suitable learning rates, along with the assumptions of the MDP setting. They do not transfer automatically to a deep network trained on a finite replay buffer. REINFORCE and actor–critic methods developed another route by directly adjusting action probabilities.

Research on dopamine responses found relationships with reward-prediction errors, including shifts in response as reward-predicting cues are learned. This is evidence connecting some biological learning signals to computational models, not a claim that every dopamine signal implements one RL algorithm or that an RL objective explains all behavior.

DQN combined learned visual representations with Q-learning, experience replay, and a target network. The [2015 Nature paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature14236) evaluated 49 Atari games using a common algorithm and architecture, with a separately trained agent for each game. Performance varied across games; one jointly trained model did not outperform humans on all 49. The significant result was that one learning setup could address many tasks from high-dimensional observations.

AlphaGo combined learned policies and values with search, including human-game training and self-play. AlphaZero removed the requirement for human-game examples in its training setup while retaining game rules and substantial computation. MuZero learned a model useful for predicting reward, value, and policy during planning; it did not need to reconstruct every detail of the environment. These examples connect learning, representation, and planning rather than eliminating the need for design choices.

TRPO and PPO addressed policy-update stability. PPO's clipping changes the optimization incentive for moving action probabilities far from the behavior policy; it is not a hard guarantee that performance will improve. Christiano and colleagues' 2017 preference-learning work, followed by language-model applications such as InstructGPT, used learned feedback to supply an objective for RL. The preference model and the resulting policy remain separate objects to evaluate.

Offline RL studies fixed datasets, model-based RL uses learned dynamics or prediction models, and multi-agent RL studies interacting learners. Each changes the information available for improving a policy. A dataset may contain little evidence about an attractive new action; a learned model may be wrong where a planner chooses to visit; other learning agents may change the effective environment. These are central learning problems, not details a larger network automatically resolves.

#### The MDP Framework, Value Functions, and Policy Learning

#### Markov Decision Processes: The Formal Foundation

A finite discounted MDP specifies states, available actions, transition probabilities `P(s′|s,a)`, expected immediate reward `R(s,a)`, and a discount `0 ≤ γ < 1`. A policy `π(a|s)` gives action probabilities. The Markov assumption says the state contains the history needed to predict the next transition and reward given an action. Whether a sensor observation contains that information is a modeling question.

The return is a sum of rewards over time, such as `Gₜ = Rₜ₊₁ + γRₜ₊₂ + γ²Rₜ₊₃ + …`. The state value `V^π(s)` is expected return when starting at `s` and following `π`; `Q^π(s,a)` first takes action `a`, then follows `π`. The star in `V*` or `Q*` instead denotes optimal value. Reward, sampled return, estimated value, and optimal value should not be used interchangeably.

The optimality equation is `V*(s) = max_a [R(s,a) + γ Σ_s′ P(s′|s,a)V*(s′)]`. In a finite MDP with bounded rewards and discount below one, the Bellman optimality operator is a contraction and has a unique value-function fixed point. Value iteration approaches it; an exact optimum need not be reached after a fixed finite number of iterations. Episodic undiscounted and average-reward objectives use different conditions.

For a small example, one action ends the episode with reward 3. Another gives reward 0 now and leads to a state where the next action ends with reward 5. With `γ=0.9`, the second choice is worth `0 + 0.9 × 5 = 4.5`, so it is preferable despite giving no immediate reward. This example can be solved by planning if the transitions are known; learning is needed when their values must be estimated from experience.

A partially observed process can still have Markovian underlying states. The agent may need a history summary or a belief distribution over states to choose well. If two situations look identical but require different actions, simply using the current observation as the MDP state can be inadequate. Adding memory changes the representation available to the policy.

#### Value-Based and Policy-Based Methods

A tabular Q-learning update moves an estimate toward `y = r + γ max_a′ Q(s′,a′)`: `Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[y−Q(s,a)]`. At a terminal transition the target is just the reward. If the old estimate is 2, reward is 1, the next state's largest estimate is 4, `γ=0.9`, and `α=0.5`, the target is 4.6 and the new estimate is 3.3. The target includes an estimate, so errors can propagate as well as useful information.

DQN represents Q-values with a neural network. Experience replay reuses stored transitions and reduces dependence between nearby training samples; it does not make the entire dataset independent. A slowly updated target network reduces how rapidly bootstrap targets change. These mechanisms help training, without extending tabular convergence guarantees to every network or dataset.

Policy-gradient methods instead adjust a parameterized policy directly. For a finite-horizon undiscounted episodic objective, one form of the gradient is `E[Σₜ ∇θ log πθ(aₜ|sₜ)(Gₜ−b(sₜ))]`, where `Gₜ` is the remaining sampled return. An action-independent baseline `b(sₜ)` can reduce variance without changing the expected gradient under the usual assumptions. Actor–critic methods learn a value estimate for this purpose and often use bootstrapped advantage estimates, introducing their own bias–variance tradeoff. Discounted objectives require matching discount conventions in the estimator.

On-policy learning evaluates or improves the policy supplying the relevant data. Off-policy learning can use data from another behavior policy, with algorithm-specific requirements. It enables reuse but does not make arbitrary old data sufficient: coverage and distribution mismatch matter. Function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy training can interact to cause instability or divergence.

PPO commonly collects data with a policy, then performs a limited number of updates using ratios of new to old action probabilities. Its clipped objective discourages some excessively large changes. Clipping is not a hard constraint on every ratio or on total policy divergence, and does not guarantee monotonic improvement. The [PPO documentation](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/algorithms/ppo.html) explains why implementations also monitor approximate KL divergence and may stop an update early.

#### Credit Assignment, Exploration, and Sample Efficiency

One-step TD updates the value of a visited state using the next reward and value estimate. Repeated experience can carry information back to earlier states. Multi-step returns include more observed rewards before bootstrapping. Eligibility traces keep a decaying record of past visits, allowing a TD error to update multiple earlier estimates; TD(λ) relates this to a weighted mixture of return lengths. These methods differ in variance, bias, and when information becomes available.

Exploration determines which evidence is collected. An ε-greedy policy occasionally chooses a random action, but sparse-reward problems may require a coordinated sequence that such sampling rarely discovers. Optimism, uncertainty estimates, count-based bonuses, or learned novelty signals can encourage exploration. A prediction-error bonus can also reward inherently unpredictable observations, so “surprising” is not automatically “useful to learn.”

Sample efficiency measures learning relative to environment experience, which differs from computation time. A model-based method may use extra computation to learn and plan through a dynamics model, saving interactions when that model is useful. Planning can also exploit model errors. Offline RL faces a related problem when a policy chooses actions poorly represented in its fixed dataset: high predicted value may reflect extrapolation rather than evidence.

Evaluate the interaction budget, computation, reward definition, and policies used to collect data. Keep evaluation episodes separate from training exploration and report results across seeds and tasks. Distinguish actual episode termination from a time-limit truncation when constructing bootstrap targets. That implementation detail changes the learning problem.

#### What Studying This Changes

You should be able to define state, observation, action, reward, policy, and return for a small task, and explain what is known versus learned. A simulator does not remove modeling assumptions; it makes them executable.

Solve a tiny MDP by value iteration, then learn it with tabular Q-learning and compare the estimates with the known solution. Change the discount, reward timing, exploration, and observation representation separately. This shows which changes alter the objective and which change the learner's ability to find a solution.

Treat reward design and evaluation as separate responsibilities. A learner may exploit a proxy, fail to optimize it, or encounter a different environment. “The agent maximizes exactly what it was told” overlooks optimization and generalization failures. Inspect trajectories and test whether improved return corresponds to the intended result, especially when using learned feedback.
