| Treating preference reward as solved alignment | The reward model can be biased or inaccurate where the policy seeks high scores. | Evaluate policy outcomes independently and inspect reward-model failures. |
| Ignoring experience costs and coverage | A large number of updates cannot create evidence about unseen actions. | Report interaction budgets and test policies outside well-covered training cases. |

### 5.5 — Large Language Models and Foundation Models

An autoregressive language model assigns probabilities to token sequences by predicting each token from preceding tokens: `p(x₁:T) = Πₜ p(xₜ|x₍<t₎)`. Tokens are units defined by a tokenizer and need not be whole words or single characters. Predicting text can require useful representations of syntax, facts, and relationships, but next-token training alone does not specify every behavior of a deployed assistant.

Separate the pretrained model, its post-training, its inference procedure, and the surrounding application. Instruction examples and preference feedback can change model parameters; a prompt and retrieved documents change the context; a tool can perform a calculation or query an external system. These mechanisms provide different information and different grounds for trusting an answer.

A foundation model is pretrained for reuse across a range of downstream tasks through prompting, adaptation, or integration into larger systems. The category includes language, vision, speech, and multimodal models. It describes a pattern of reuse, not a guarantee of universal competence. Transfer learning existed before the term; scale and reusable interfaces expanded the range of practical applications.

*Prerequisites: Training and evaluation (§5.2), deep-learning architectures (§5.3), and basic probability (§2.5). RL (§5.4) helps explain some post-training methods, but is not required to understand every language model.*

#### From Word Vectors to Generalist Systems

Language modeling has long used context. An n-gram model estimates a word or token from a limited preceding window, while smoothing handles sparse counts. Sparse features, grammars, probabilistic models, and learned distributed representations coexisted before the transformer. The historical problem was how to share evidence across related contexts while handling long dependencies and limited data.

Neural language models learned vector representations before word2vec. Word2vec's 2013 methods made learning useful word vectors from local prediction objectives efficient at larger scale. Their usual static embedding assigns one vector to a word type, so different senses are not separately represented by the lookup alone. Some analogies correspond to useful vector relationships; this is not a general theorem that semantic relations are linear or reliably recovered by vector arithmetic.

The 2014 sequence-to-sequence work used recurrent encoder–decoder models for variable-length mappings. Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio's attention work let a decoder consult different encoder positions instead of relying solely on one fixed summary. The transformer in 2017 reorganized these interactions around attention. The change concerned information access and parallel computation, not the first recognition that context affects meaning.

BERT used bidirectional context in masked-token prediction, while the original GPT used left-to-right language modeling. Both investigated reusing pretrained representations for downstream tasks. GPT-2 and GPT-3 expanded autoregressive modeling and studied transfer through text prompts, including demonstrations supplied in context. In-context learning changes the model's computation for a particular input without the usual gradient update to its weights; its success depends on the task, model, examples, and prompt.

Scaling studies, including Kaplan's work and Chinchilla (§5.3), examined how to allocate parameters, data, and training compute. Their findings made the training budget explicit. They did not establish that one parameter count determines competence, or that improving a text-prediction loss guarantees factual reliability. Open-weight releases also enabled independent adaptation and experiments, subject to the information and licensing provided with each release.

Instruction tuning and preference training changed how pretrained models responded to requests. InstructGPT documented a pipeline using demonstrations, preference comparisons, a reward model, and policy optimization. DPO later derived a direct preference objective under a related regularized formulation. These methods train behavior from particular examples and judgments; they do not remove disagreements about what a good response is or independently certify its truth.

Retrieval, tool use, and additional inference computation expanded the design space beyond a single model call. A system can search documents, run generated code, generate multiple candidates, or use a checker to select or revise an answer. Longer deliberation and repeated sampling are not equivalent to a specified search algorithm. Their benefit depends on whether the additional computation obtains useful evidence or identifies mistakes.

The resulting application has several independently changeable parts: model weights, prompt and context, retrieval, decoding, tools, and verification. This explains why a model benchmark and an application evaluation can give different results. Historical progress in models and progress in the systems built around them should be distinguished when comparing capabilities.

#### Architecture, Training, Adaptation, and Evaluation

#### The Transformer and Its Scaling Properties

A transformer turns token embeddings and positional information into contextual representations. In one attention head, queries and keys produce scores, softmax converts the permitted scores to weights, and those weights combine value vectors. With scalar values 2 and 10 and weights 0.75 and 0.25, the result is 4. This is a weighted computation, not a probability that a source statement is true. Multiple heads provide different learned projections, followed by further mixing and nonlinear computation.

In a causal decoder, the representation at position `t` may use positions up to and including `t`, and is trained to predict token `t+1`. A mask prevents access to later target tokens. The entire training sequence is already available, so many position-wise losses can be computed in parallel. During ordinary autoregressive generation, the next token must be selected before the following prediction can use it. Training parallelism does not remove this generation dependency.

Cross-entropy training increases the probability assigned to observed targets. For a fixed target distribution, minimizing cross-entropy is equivalent to minimizing its KL divergence to the model, up to the target entropy. In practice this is estimated from finite selected data. Tokenization, document boundaries, filtering, and which positions contribute loss all change the learning problem.

Dense attention requires quadratic pairwise work in sequence length for fixed feature dimensions. [FlashAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135) changes memory access and computation scheduling to avoid storing the full attention matrix in high-bandwidth memory while computing exact attention. It does not turn all-pairs attention into linear arithmetic work. During generation, a key–value cache stores previous projections, trading memory for avoided recomputation. Context capacity, successful use of distant information, and inference latency are separate measurements.

Transformer blocks also contain residual connections, normalization, and position-wise feed-forward transformations; attention alone is not the whole model. Mixtures of experts can increase total parameter capacity while activating selected experts for each token, but routing, load balance, memory, and communication remain costs. Model size by itself is therefore an incomplete description of inference work.

#### Pretraining, Fine-tuning, and Alignment

Pretraining determines much of the model's initial repertoire. Data selection includes domains, languages, duplicates, quality criteria, document boundaries, and contamination checks. More tokens and more independently useful information are not the same thing. The tokenizer also affects which patterns are easy to express and how much context and computation a piece of text consumes.

Supervised instruction tuning trains on examples of requests and responses. A preference-based pipeline may instead collect comparisons, fit a reward model, and optimize the policy against that model with a reference-policy penalty. Such a penalty limits incentives to move far from the reference under the chosen objective; it does not guarantee that reward hacking, factual error, or sycophancy is prevented. Human judgments can themselves reflect ambiguity, limited expertise, and presentation preferences.

[Direct Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290) fits a policy using preferred and dispreferred responses and their probability ratios relative to a reference model. It avoids separately fitting and optimizing an explicit reward model in the original setup. The labels, coverage, and objective still matter, so a simpler training pipeline is not evidence that preference misspecification has disappeared.

Adaptation methods change different parts of a system:

| Method | What changes | What it can supply |
|---|---|---|
| Prompting or in-context examples | Input context | Task instructions, demonstrations, and temporary information |
| Retrieval-augmented generation | Documents selected into context | Evidence from an external collection, subject to retrieval and reading quality |
| Fine-tuning, including LoRA | Model parameters or added trainable parameters | Learned changes in behavior or task performance from training examples |
| Tool use | Computation or access outside the model | A calculation, database result, or action governed by the tool's interface |

LoRA trains low-rank parameter updates; it reduces some training costs without making the base model's storage and computation disappear. Retrieval does not guarantee that a source is correct, current, or faithfully used. A tool result provides evidence only for what the tool actually checked. Combining methods is useful when each addresses an identified failure, with the complete system evaluated afterward.

#### Evaluation: What Models Can and Cannot Do

Define the evaluated system: model and version, prompt, context, tools, sampling, retries, and computation budget. A one-attempt answer and a result selected from many attempts are different measurements. Benchmarks such as MMLU, HumanEval, and mathematical problem sets test particular tasks under particular scoring rules; their names do not supply a general capability guarantee.

For a toy illustration, if independently sampled candidates each succeed with probability `p`, the probability that at least one of `k` candidates succeeds is `1−(1−p)^k`. With `p=0.2` and `k=5`, it is about 67.2%, compared with 20% for one attempt. This is an opportunity for a selector, not the success rate of an actual system unless it can identify the correct candidate. Evaluation must include the checker's errors, candidate dependence, and total cost.

Inspect contamination, near-duplicate tasks, prompt sensitivity, distribution changes, and per-category errors. Calibration compares stated probabilities with observed correctness under a defined task; token probabilities are not automatically calibrated probabilities that a proposition is true. Different phrasings can divide probability among equivalent answers. Verbal confidence also requires empirical calibration rather than being accepted at face value.

For grounded answers, test whether cited passages support the claims, not only whether citations exist. For generated code, tests provide evidence for tested behavior and may miss specification errors. For structured output, constrained decoding can enforce a format while leaving its contents wrong. Evaluate retrieval, generation, verification, and any external action together, because an error at one stage can invalidate otherwise correct later work.

#### What Studying This Changes

You should be able to locate a proposed improvement in the system: changing weights, supplying context, allocating more inference work, obtaining external evidence, or checking an output. These interventions solve different problems and have different costs.

Build a small document-question-answering task with answerable and unanswerable questions. Compare a base prompt, supplied passages, and a retrieval pipeline using the same questions. Inspect retrieval misses, unsupported claims, and abstentions separately. A higher overall score is more informative when you can identify which stage improved.

For a difficult task, compare one attempt with several attempts under a fixed total budget and a specified selection method. Record latency and cost alongside correctness. This makes the capability–reliability distinction concrete: producing a correct candidate sometimes is different from reliably delivering a correct final result.

#### Traps

| Trap | Why it misleads | Better response |
|---|---|---|
| Treating API access as an explanation | A response hides training, prompting, decoding, and external system choices. | Describe the full inference setup and which component supplies each piece of evidence. |
| Comparing scores without budgets or selection rules | Retries, tools, and candidate selection can change performance substantially. | Compare complete procedures at a stated cost and evaluate the selector. |
| Treating factual error as either inevitable everywhere or solved by prompting | Error rates depend on task, evidence, training, and checking; fluent output alone is insufficient. | Measure unsupported claims and test retrieval, verification, and abstention. |
| Ignoring pretraining and adaptation data | Coverage, duplication, filtering, and labels shape what can be learned. | Examine data provenance and evaluate unfamiliar cases. |
| Treating preference training as a complete reliability measure | Approval and correctness can diverge, and the application may perform actions beyond answering. | Evaluate intended outcomes and the permissions and checks around actions. |
| Equating open weights with full transparency | Weights may be available without training data, complete recipes, or an understood mechanism. | Identify which artifacts are available and which conclusions they support. |

### 5.6 — Interpretability and Mechanistic Interpretability

Interpretability asks for understandable, testable accounts of a model's behavior. Different questions require different methods: which inputs affect a prediction, what information can be recovered from a representation, which internal computations contribute to an output, and whether an explanation helps a person detect errors. A method useful for one question may not answer the others.

Mechanistic interpretability investigates the computations inside a learned model. It forms hypotheses about representations and pathways, then tests them with measurements and interventions. The goal is to explain specified behavior at a useful level of detail. A meaningful feature label or an attractive visualization is a starting hypothesis, not a complete account of the computation.

Internal analysis can complement behavioral testing by locating a failure mechanism or predicting a new failure case. It does not automatically establish reliability on every input. An understandable model can still implement an unsuitable objective, and some properties of a complicated model can be checked without understanding every learned feature. The relevant question is what claim the available evidence supports.

*Prerequisites: Neural-network computation and gradients (§5.3), basic experimental evaluation (§5.2), and transformer structure (§5.5) for the language-model examples. Begin with a small model whose activations and outputs can be inspected directly.*

#### From Feature Visualization to Mechanistic Understanding

Explaining a model did not begin with recent transformer research. Statistical modeling, rule systems, decision trees, sensitivity analysis, and neural-network visualization supplied different traditions. Expert systems could show a rule trace, but the trace still depended on the adequacy of the encoded knowledge. Learned models raised an additional question: how can their acquired representations and computations be described after training?

Feature visualization searches for inputs that activate a unit or direction, often by optimizing an input while regularizing it toward interpretable patterns. Work summarized in Distill's 2017 articles made the method and its choices accessible. Optimized images and naturally occurring high-activation examples provide complementary evidence; either can be misleading if the analysis selects only examples fitting a preferred interpretation.

The Circuits work in 2020 connected feature observations to compositions of computations in convolutional networks. The 2021 transformer-circuits framework analyzed how attention heads and other components read and write representations in the residual stream. This supplied explicit algebra and candidate mechanisms for studying particular architectures. It did not establish that every model uses the same set of human-named components.

The 2022 [induction-head study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11895) investigated a pattern-completion mechanism associated with in-context learning. The authors distinguished strong causal evidence in small attention-only models from correlational evidence in larger models with MLPs. That distinction matters: explaining one pattern-completion behavior does not establish one mechanism for all learning from context.

Superposition research examined how several features may be represented by overlapping directions. Sparse autoencoders then offered a way to fit a sparse dictionary to recorded activations. The 2023 monosemanticity work and [2024 experiments on Claude 3 Sonnet](https://www.anthropic.com/research/mapping-mind-language-model) found interpretable candidate features and tested some by steering activations. These results expanded the scale of investigation while leaving questions about completeness, interpretation, and side effects.

The 2025 [Circuit Tracing work](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2025/attribution-graphs/methods.html) used more interpretable replacement components to build attribution graphs and investigate selected behaviors, including in a deployed model. The replacement is an approximation whose faithfulness must be evaluated. It would be inaccurate to say that circuit analysis is confined to tiny models, or that these advances amount to a complete explanation of a production model.

#### Features, Circuits, and the Limits of What Can Be Known

#### What Features Models Represent

A feature is a proposed property represented by some aspect of a model's state. Many methods look for linear directions in an activation space because they are tractable and often useful. This is a modeling hypothesis, not a theorem that every concept is linear, localized, or aligned with a single neuron. Features may be distributed, nonlinear, or dependent on context.

Polysemanticity means that one unit responds in several apparently different contexts. Superposition is a possible representational mechanism: multiple features use overlapping directions, allowing economical representation when only a few are active together, at a cost of interference. Polysemantic observations alone do not prove that a particular superposition model explains them.

A sparse autoencoder approximates an activation vector with `a ≈ Dz + b`, where the columns of `D` form a learned dictionary and `z` has relatively few active coefficients. One objective combines reconstruction error with a sparsity penalty, such as `‖a−(Dz+b)‖² + λ‖z‖₁`. Dictionary size, sparsity, training data, and optimization influence the decomposition. A feature may split across dictionary elements, and some behaviorally important information may remain in the reconstruction error.

Assess candidate features using diverse positive and negative examples, held-out activations, and interventions. A probe that predicts a property from activations shows that information is recoverable by that probe; it does not establish that the original model uses it for the output under study. Steering a direction can show an effect, but changes in unrelated outputs or unnatural activation states may complicate the interpretation. Automated labels for features are hypotheses to evaluate.

#### Circuits: How Features Compose

A circuit is a proposed subset of computations contributing to a specified behavior. Defining the behavior comes first: repeating a token pattern, resolving a name in a sentence, or selecting one answer over another. The same model can use different pathways on different inputs, and several pathways may redundantly support one behavior.

A simple induction mechanism completes `[A][B] … [A]` with `[B]`. In a two-layer construction, a previous-token head can place information about `[A]` at the position containing `[B]`. At the later `[A]`, another head can match that previous-token information and copy information about `[B]`. This explains a particular way to reuse an observed association. It does not establish that all in-context tasks reduce to copying or that every large model implements this exact construction.

Activation patching tests such hypotheses by replacing selected internal activations from one run with those from another. Consider sentences differing only in whether Alice gives a book to Bob or to Carol, followed by a question about the recipient. If patching selected activations restores preference for Bob in the Carol run, that is evidence that the patched computation can mediate this output difference. It does not prove that the fact is stored permanently in that one location or that the pathway is uniquely necessary.

Use matched prompts, align token positions, specify the output metric, and compare interventions at unrelated locations. Zero ablation, mean ablation, and replacement with another input's activations create different conditions. An intervention may push the model away from naturally occurring states. Test the proposed circuit on new cases and examine both what its removal disrupts and what its retained computation can reproduce. A plausible graph becomes an explanation through these checks.

#### What Can and Cannot Be Verified

Separate observation, prediction, intervention, and generalization. A component correlating with a behavior is an observation. Predicting how an intervention will change that behavior is a stronger hypothesis. Confirming the prediction supports a causal claim within the experiment. Testing new inputs assesses how far the account extends. None of these steps automatically supplies a global safety guarantee.

Gradient saliency measures local sensitivity under a chosen parameterization; it need not describe the effect of a large input change. Attention weights describe one part of information routing, while value vectors and other paths also affect the output. A language model's written explanation is itself an output, not a privileged readout of the computation that produced the answer. Each can be useful evidence when paired with an appropriate test.

For dictionary or replacement-model methods, measure reconstruction quality and downstream behavioral fidelity as well as interpretability of the labels. Explain which components remain unanalyzed and how much of the target behavior is recovered. Simpler surrogate explanations may omit interactions that matter outside the tested examples.

Keep the scientific claim narrow enough to challenge: which model checkpoint, which behavior, which input family, which interventions, and which competing explanations? A failure on a new case can improve the hypothesis. An account that explains every possible outcome after the fact is difficult to test and offers little predictive value.

#### What Studying This Changes

You should be able to state what an interpretability experiment is trying to explain and what evidence would count against the explanation. Distinguish information recoverable from a representation from information the model demonstrably uses in a tested computation.

Begin with a small repeated-token task or a controlled name-resolution task. Record the baseline behavior, formulate a circuit hypothesis, run interventions and controls, then evaluate new examples. Preserve failed interventions as well as successful visualizations; they constrain which explanation is credible.

Use internal analysis together with ordinary evaluation. A proposed mechanism can suggest new tests, and behavioral failures can guide where to inspect the model. Interpretability is most useful when it improves a concrete prediction or diagnosis, rather than supplying a reassuring label for an otherwise untested system.

**Books and Survey Articles**

Distill's **Feature Visualization** and **Circuits** articles show how visual examples and interventions can support hypotheses about neural computation. Keep the distinction between describing a feature and showing how the model uses it.

For transformers, read **“A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits”** after you can follow an attention layer in code. Study the induction-head and superposition papers with their toy experiments, then examine what changes when sparse autoencoders are applied to larger models. Lipton's **“The Mythos of Model Interpretability”** helps clarify what different authors mean by an explanation. None of these methods should be assessed only by how convincing its visualization looks.

| Equating a saliency map with a mechanism | Local sensitivity does not uniquely identify a computation or explain large changes. | Specify the claim and compare it with perturbations and internal interventions. |

| Skipping intervention controls | A large effect may arise from unnatural activations or unrelated disruption. | Compare matched interventions, alternative baselines, and new input families. |
| Generalizing a local circuit explanation to overall safety | The model can use other pathways or fail for reasons outside the analyzed behavior. | State coverage and combine internal evidence with system-level evaluation. |

### 5.7 — AI Safety and Alignment

AI safety studies how to identify, evaluate, and reduce harms associated with AI systems. Alignment concerns how a system's objectives and behavior relate to intended goals, human preferences, and relevant constraints. Whose intentions count, how conflicts are resolved, and who bears an error's consequences are part of the problem; matching one user's request is not a complete definition of safety.

Separate failure mechanisms. A model may optimize an inadequate proxy, make an ordinary prediction error, fail under changed conditions, be used for a harmful purpose, or be compromised through its surrounding software. These mechanisms call for different evidence and interventions. Training a more preferred response does not automatically correct permissions, data access, or an unreliable downstream action.

The subject connects learning (§5.2–5.5) with security (§4.5), verification (§3.6), and system reliability (§4.10). It also includes contested hypotheses about future systems. Distinguishing observed failures, controlled demonstrations, theoretical arguments, and forecasts makes the discussion more precise and keeps technical questions connected to evidence.

*Prerequisites: Learning objectives and evaluation (§5.2), sequential decision problems (§5.4), and language-model systems (§5.5). Interpretability (§5.6) supplies one possible source of evidence, alongside testing, verification, and system controls.*

#### From Early Warnings to Technical Discipline

Concerns about automated decisions have several histories. Control engineering, dependable software, robotics, and human factors studied failures in systems acting on the world. Wiener warned that a machine's specified purpose could differ from the purpose people actually wanted. His concern connects naturally to specification and feedback; it did not require a prediction that a particular future AI architecture would exist.

I. J. Good's 1965 discussion of an intelligence explosion considered the possibility of systems improving the design of their successors. Later arguments about highly capable systems and control, including Bostrom's work, developed conditional scenarios. Their conclusions depend on assumptions about capability, goals, autonomy, and the dynamics of improvement. Historical influence and empirical confirmation are different questions.

As learning systems became more widely used, researchers also investigated concrete failure mechanisms. The 2016 paper [Concrete Problems in AI Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.06565) organized five problems: avoiding side effects, avoiding reward hacking, scalable supervision, safe exploration, and distributional shift. These connected objective design, feedback cost, and learning conditions to unwanted behavior. The list was a research agenda, not a complete inventory of harms.

Preference learning supplied an alternative to hand-writing every reward. Christiano and colleagues' 2017 work learned feedback from comparisons and used it to train behavior. Later language-model work, including InstructGPT and Constitutional AI, explored demonstrations, comparisons, and written principles in post-training. These experiments showed measurable behavioral changes under particular evaluations. They did not establish that every relevant value could be inferred from comparisons or that the resulting systems were safe in every application.

Deployment broadened the unit of analysis from a model's output to an application with users, data, tools, and institutions. Work on model cards, incident documentation, red-teaming, and capability evaluations developed ways to describe uses, limitations, and observed failures. The [NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) treats risk management as an organizational process as well as a technical measurement problem.

Scalable oversight and learned-objective research ask how supervision might remain effective when outputs become difficult to judge or behavior changes beyond training. Some studies use deliberately constructed models or restricted tasks to test proposed failure mechanisms. Such experiments can identify possibilities and challenge methods, while estimating their prevalence in other systems requires further evidence. A useful history follows how questions became measurable without treating either reassurance or catastrophe as a predetermined conclusion.

#### Specification, Oversight, and the Empirical Safety of Deployed Systems

#### The Specification Problem

A training objective is an operational specification of some desired behavior. Its adequacy depends on the task. Suppose a support assistant is rewarded for closing tickets quickly. It can improve that metric by resolving problems efficiently, but also by marking unresolved requests as complete. “Ticket closed” and “problem resolved” are different variables. The example exposes a missing requirement without requiring the system to possess a human-like intention to cheat.

Reward hacking or specification gaming describes behavior that scores well under a proxy while violating the intended outcome. Goodhart-style effects are a useful family of explanations: selection and optimization can favor cases where a measure stops tracking the goal well. This is a possible failure mechanism, not a theorem that every objective is unusable or every sufficiently capable learner must exploit it. Some narrowly defined tasks admit precise specifications and strong checks.

Distinguish three failures: optimizing the wrong objective, failing to optimize the chosen objective, and learning behavior that changes undesirably outside the training setting. They can look similar in an output while requiring different remedies. Claims that a learned model has acquired an internal objective require evidence about its behavior or computation; a single bad answer is not sufficient to establish such a mechanism.

Feedback methods add information but retain assumptions. Preference comparisons depend on the raters, instructions, and examples; written principles require interpretation in context; a reward model extrapolates beyond its labels. Separate user approval from correctness, and task completion from acceptable side effects. For the ticket example, evaluate verified resolution, reopening rates, and inappropriate closure alongside speed, and specify when a human must make the decision.

#### Scalable Oversight and the Verification Gap

Oversight becomes difficult when checking an output requires scarce expertise, substantial computation, or observing delayed consequences. Verification can be cheaper than generation for some tasks, but not all. A proof checker can validate a derivation against formal rules; it cannot establish that the theorem formalized the user's intended claim unless that correspondence is also checked.

Task decomposition, tool-assisted checking, expert review, and random audits can increase supervision capacity. They work only when the pieces retain the information needed for a reliable judgment. A set of individually plausible summaries can omit a decisive cross-document contradiction. A reviewer aided by an unreliable model can also inherit its mistakes.

Debate proposes using competing arguments to help a judge identify errors. Its effectiveness depends on what evidence can be exposed and what the judge can evaluate; persuasive performance does not guarantee truth. Iterated amplification uses assisted judgments to train stronger systems. These are research approaches with particular experimental and theoretical assumptions, not established general solutions.

The [weak-to-strong generalization study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.09390) tested whether a stronger pretrained model could learn from weaker model labels on selected tasks. Improvements over the weak supervisor showed that imperfect labels need not impose an identical performance ceiling, while gaps from stronger supervision remained. This is an empirical analogy to a supervision problem, not a demonstration that arbitrary more-capable systems can be reliably aligned by weaker overseers.

Evaluate the supervisor as well as the model: which errors does it detect, which does it share, what information does it have, and what does review cost? Better oversight should improve a measured judgment or outcome. Agreement among several evaluators is weaker evidence when they share training data, assumptions, or failure modes.

#### Empirical Safety of Deployed Systems

Evaluate the deployed system under a stated use and threat model. Identify what information it can read, what actions it can take, and what happens after a mistaken output. An assistant that drafts a proposed refund and one that can execute it have different consequences even if their text-generation accuracy is identical.

Prompt injection concerns instructions arriving through material that should be treated as data, such as a retrieved page or tool result. Refusal training alone does not establish a trustworthy boundary between that material and authorized instructions. Limit tool permissions, validate proposed operations in application code, and keep sensitive actions behind controls appropriate to the task. Jailbreak resistance, access control, and factual accuracy are related but different properties.

Unsupported claims and sycophancy require direct evaluation. Retrieval can supply evidence but may retrieve irrelevant or manipulated material; fluent summaries can still misstate it. Preference training can reward pleasing presentation, but sycophancy has no single necessary cause. Use factual checks, counterexamples, uncertainty evaluation, and abstention criteria matched to the application. Error reduction is a measurable goal; neither “this can never be fixed” nor “the model was aligned” replaces a test.

Capability evaluations ask what a system can accomplish under particular access, assistance, and time budgets. Misuse risk additionally depends on who can access it, what other resources are available, and whether the capability changes an actor's practical options. Controlled demonstrations, realistic task evaluations, and incident observations provide different evidence. A failed attempt by one evaluator does not establish that no other procedure would succeed.

Zero observed failures does not imply zero risk. In a simple model of 1,000 independent tests drawn from one fixed deployment distribution, with zero failures, a one-sided 95% binomial upper confidence bound on the failure probability is `1−0.05^(1/1000) ≈ 0.003`. Even this statement depends on the sampling model; correlated tests or changed inputs can invalidate its interpretation. Report what was tested, the failure definition, uncertainty, and which uses remain outside the evaluation.

Monitoring and incident response extend evaluation after release. Track meaningful outcomes, investigate failures, revise controls, and check whether mitigations introduce new errors or burdens. A model change, new tool, or new user population can change the assumptions of an earlier assessment. Safety evidence belongs to a versioned system in a use setting, not permanently to a model name.

#### What Studying This Changes

You should be able to turn a broad safety claim into an assessable one: a specified system, users and affected parties, permitted actions, failure conditions, and supporting evidence. Distinguish an objective-design problem from an implementation defect, a distribution shift, or an access-control failure.

For a small assistant application, write down one intended outcome, one tempting proxy, and one counterexample where they diverge. Test the model and the surrounding controls separately. Record which interventions improve the intended outcome, not merely the proxy or the apparent confidence of the answer.

Read research claims according to their evidence. A theorem has assumptions; a controlled demonstration establishes a possibility under its setup; a benchmark estimates performance under a protocol; a forecast adds uncertain extrapolation. Comparing these carefully makes it possible to investigate future risks and present failures without treating either as a substitute for the other.

#### Resources

**Books and Texts**

Russell's **Human Compatible** develops an argument for treating human objectives as uncertain rather than fixed and fully known. Christian's **The Alignment Problem** presents the history and human consequences of learning systems. Bostrom's **Superintelligence** develops conditional arguments about highly capable systems and control; distinguish those arguments from measurements of existing systems and from forecasts about when such systems will exist.

For technical study, start with **“Concrete Problems in AI Safety”** and the preference-learning papers, then read Ngo, Chan, and Mindermann on deep learning alignment and Casper et al. on RLHF limitations. Hubinger et al. develops the learned-optimization concern. For each proposed failure, identify the mechanism, assumptions, supporting experiments, and what evidence would weaken the claim.

| Reducing safety to output moderation | Harms can arise from wrong decisions, tool permissions, data handling, or delayed effects. | Evaluate the whole system and the consequences of its permitted actions. |

| Accepting or dismissing future-risk claims without examining assumptions | Forecasts combine mechanisms with uncertain claims about future capabilities and deployment. | Separate assumptions, evidence for mechanisms, and uncertainty about extrapolation. |
| Reading only one research viewpoint | Different approaches prioritize different harms and make different assumptions. | Compare arguments, empirical tests, and the interests of affected parties. |
| Separating safety from system design | Permissions, objectives, interfaces, and recovery procedures shape consequences. | Evaluate these choices during development and after material changes. |
| Treating all evidence as interchangeable | A demonstration, a test score, a theorem, and a forecast support different conclusions. | State the type and scope of evidence behind each claim. |

## Chapter 6 — Applied Computer Science Domains

### 6.1 — Computer Graphics and Visual Computing

Computer graphics constructs images and other visual representations by computation. A renderer takes a scene description—geometry, materials, lights, and a camera—and estimates the image that this scene would produce. Modeling and animation specify the scene and its changes over time. Visualization also asks how to encode data so that a viewer can understand it; a useful image need not be a physically realistic one.

A beginner can separate three questions: what is represented, what image is requested, and how much computation is available? A triangle mesh describes surfaces; a camera specifies a projection; a rendering algorithm estimates visibility and appearance. Changing one can alter the image without changing the others. This separation helps locate errors instead of treating a wrong-looking image as one undifferentiated graphics problem.

Visual computing connects graphics to image processing and computer vision. Rendering predicts an image from a scene; reconstruction tries to infer a scene from images. The latter is generally ambiguous: several combinations of shape, material, and lighting can explain similar observations. Learned representations (§5.3) add useful methods, while geometry, sampling, and camera models remain important.

*Prerequisites: Linear algebra (§2.3) for coordinates and transformations; calculus (§2.4) and probability (§2.5) for light transport and sampling. Basic programming is enough to begin drawing and transforming simple shapes; GPU architecture (§4.1) becomes useful when studying performance.*

#### From Oscilloscopes to Neural Radiance Fields

Interactive graphics developed from earlier work on electronic displays, plotting, and real-time systems. Sutherland's 1963 Sketchpad was an influential demonstration of drawing and editing geometric objects with a light pen. It stored objects and relationships rather than only marks on a display. A constraint such as keeping two lines perpendicular could survive an edit. The distinction between a model and its displayed image made graphical interaction more useful.

As raster displays spread, visibility and shading became separate computational problems: which surface contributes to a sample, and what color should it contribute? Gouraud shading interpolated vertex colors; Phong shading interpolated normals before evaluating lighting. Phong also proposed a reflection model, which is a different idea from the interpolation method. Smoother interpolation improved appearance without adding geometric detail or solving all light transport.

Appel's and Whitted's ray-tracing work showed how intersections and secondary rays could calculate shadows, reflections, and refractions. These effects were not impossible with rasterization; alternative techniques could approximate or construct them. Ray tracing offered a way to query geometry along arbitrary directions. Whitted-style recursive tracing and Monte Carlo path tracing are related methods with different sampling and transport capabilities.

Kajiya's 1986 rendering equation expressed outgoing surface light in terms of emission and reflected incoming light. It supported a common mathematical account of algorithms for global illumination. Veach's later work developed Monte Carlo methods for difficult transport problems. The equation is a model: the usual surface form assumes geometric optics and needs extensions for participating media or other phenomena. A renderer can accurately solve its chosen model while that model omits a physical effect.

Film rendering and interactive graphics developed under different time budgets. RenderMan supported programmable production shading, while graphics accelerators moved repeated projection, rasterization, and texture operations into hardware. Programmable shaders gave developers more control over these operations. Hardware ray-tracing support later reduced some intersection and traversal costs; it did not remove the need to budget rays, memory, and reconstruction work.

Physically based material models made it easier to reason about reflectance, energy, and lighting consistently. Pharr and Humphreys's first PBRT edition appeared in 2004; later editions with Jakob connected theory to increasingly capable implementations. Production material models also account for artistic control. Physical plausibility, speed, controllability, and a particular visual style remain different design goals.

NeRF in 2020 fitted a radiance-and-density representation from images and rendered new views by integrating along camera rays. The 2023 3D Gaussian Splatting work optimized explicit Gaussian primitives for view synthesis. Neither method is simply conventional path tracing with a new surface format. They made the dependence on capture coverage, camera estimation, and reconstruction assumptions especially visible. Generative models, denoisers, and upscalers add further tools, whose effects should be distinguished from recovering measured scene detail.

#### Rendering, Representation, and Real-Time Performance

#### The Rendering Pipeline: From Scene to Pixels

A geometric pipeline transforms object coordinates into world and camera coordinates, projects them, and determines contributions to image samples. In a simple pinhole camera looking along positive depth, with focal length 1 and image coordinates centered at the optical axis, `(x,y,z)` projects to `(x/z,y/z)`. Thus `(2,1,4)` projects to `(0.5,0.25)`. Depth changes apparent size even when the object itself is unchanged. Coordinate conventions and units must agree across the pipeline.

Rasterization determines which samples are covered by projected primitives. Attributes such as normals and texture coordinates are interpolated, and shaders calculate contributions. A depth buffer helps retain the nearest opaque surface at each sample. Fragments, samples, and displayed pixels are not identical: multiple fragments may compete, multisampling evaluates several coverage locations, and filtering combines information. Transparency and effects involving hidden surfaces need additional handling.

Ray tracing asks which geometry a ray intersects, usually using an acceleration structure such as a bounding-volume hierarchy. Shadow rays test light visibility; other rays can sample reflected or transmitted light. Tracing rays alone does not guarantee physical accuracy: material models, sampling, geometry, and which interactions are included determine the result. Hybrid renderers combine rasterization with selected ray queries.

For an opaque reflecting surface under the usual geometric-optics assumptions, outgoing radiance obeys `L_o = L_e + ∫_Ω f_r L_i cosθ dω`. Here `L_e` is emission, `f_r` is the BRDF, and the integral accumulates reflected incoming radiance over the outward hemisphere. The cosine accounts for projected area. For a Lambertian surface with reflectance `ρ`, `f_r = ρ/π`; reflectance and the value of the BRDF are not the same quantity.

Path tracing samples sequences of scattering events to estimate this transport. Monte Carlo integration weights each sampled contribution by its sampling density, which must cover the contributing region. An independent-sample estimator with finite variance has variance `σ²/n` and standard error `σ/√n`: reducing typical noise by half takes roughly four times as many samples. Unbiasedness describes the estimator under its assumptions, not every implementation. Clamping contributions, truncating paths, or denoising can introduce bias; correctly weighted Russian roulette can terminate paths without that truncation bias. [PBRT](https://pbr-book.org/4ed/Monte_Carlo_Integration) develops this sampling view.

Sampling also affects geometry and textures. A fine repeating pattern can appear as false coarse stripes when undersampled. Antialiasing estimates pixel-area contributions instead of treating one point as the whole pixel; texture filtering and mipmaps use related ideas. More pixels, more light samples, and better filtering address different errors. Identify which error is visible before increasing every quality setting.

#### Geometric Representation

A representation makes some operations easy and others expensive. Triangle meshes describe surfaces through vertices and connectivity. They support rasterization, intersection tests, and local editing, but resolving fine curvature requires more elements. Texture and normal maps can change shading detail without changing the silhouette or collision surface.

Parametric and subdivision surfaces describe smooth shapes through parameters or control meshes. Evaluating or tessellating them produces samples or polygons for rendering. Continuity and behavior near special vertices depend on the chosen construction; a compact smooth model still needs finite computation to display and intersect.

A signed distance field assigns a point's distance to a surface, with a sign distinguishing inside from outside. Under one common convention, outside is positive. From outside, sphere tracing can safely step by an exact distance or a conservative lower bound because no surface lies inside that radius. An arbitrary implicit function—or an imperfect learned distance estimate—does not automatically provide this guarantee. Numerical tolerances, thin features, and transformations require care.

NeRF uses a learned density-and-radiance field; a neural SDF instead represents a surface through distance. These are different quantities. Gaussian splatting represents appearance with positioned, oriented, colored primitives and opacity. Image-based optimization can produce useful new views without yielding the clean, watertight geometry needed for manufacturing or collision tests. Evaluate the representation for the intended operation: view synthesis, editing, relighting, simulation, or measurement.

#### GPU Architecture and Real-Time Performance

A GPU executes many work items using shared execution and memory resources. Shader invocations may process vertices, fragments, or general compute tasks. Nearby work that follows similar control flow and accesses nearby data often uses these resources efficiently. Divergence, irregular memory access, synchronization, and register pressure can reduce useful throughput; more parallel tasks do not guarantee proportional speedup.

Textures, geometry, and intermediate buffers compete for bandwidth and cache capacity. Texture units provide specialized sampling and filtering. Rendering performance can be limited by geometry processing, fragment shading, memory traffic, ray traversal, CPU submission, or synchronization. A frame capture shows which passes and resources are present; timing and profiling help determine which actually limit performance.

At 60 frames per second, the nominal frame budget is about `1000/60 ≈ 16.7 ms`. If GPU work is the limiting stage and takes 20 ms, shortening already-overlapped CPU work from 8 ms to 4 ms may leave throughput unchanged. End-to-end input latency is a separate measurement from frame throughput. Measure representative scenes and frame-time distributions, including slow frames.

Level of detail chooses representations appropriate to projected size and error. Culling avoids work that cannot affect the requested image; occlusion and transparency complicate that decision. Virtualized geometry systems such as Nanite automate parts of streaming and detail selection within supported workloads. They still have geometry, memory, material, and bandwidth costs. Validate a change by comparing both performance and visible error.

#### What Studying This Changes

You should be able to trace one point from object coordinates to an image sample and explain where visibility, material evaluation, and filtering enter. Build a small rasterizer or ray tracer, change one operation at a time, and predict the result before rendering.

For a sampling experiment, render the same scene with 100 and 400 independent samples per pixel, using the same unbiased estimator. Compare error over repeated runs against a high-quality reference. The expected reduction concerns the sampling error scale, not a guarantee that every individual pixel improves in every run.

For a performance experiment, capture a frame and identify a costly pass. Change geometry detail, shader work, or output resolution separately, then check which change moves frame time. These exercises connect linear algebra, probability, data structures, and parallel architecture to an observable result.

### 6.2 — Human-Computer Interaction and Design

Human-computer interaction studies how people use computing systems to accomplish tasks, and how those systems should be designed and evaluated. It includes the interface, the user's knowledge and abilities, the surrounding activity, and the consequences of an action. A booking form can be technically correct while leaving people unsure whether a reservation exists or how to change it.

Start with a task and the information needed to perform it. Users must discover available actions, predict their effects, carry them out, and interpret the result. A design can fail at any of these steps. Making a button more visible will not fix an unclear refund policy; explaining the policy will not fix a control that cannot be reached with a keyboard.

HCI connects implementation to psychology, design, ergonomics, and the study of social activity. Research methods help distinguish a designer's assumption from observed behavior. Visual appearance matters, but so do learnability, task success, error recovery, accessibility, and effects on people who did not choose the system.

*Prerequisites: Basic programming (§2.1) helps when building interactive prototypes. You can begin user research and paper prototyping before mastering a software framework. Probability and statistics (§2.5) become important for quantitative comparisons.*

#### From Batch Processing to Designing for Billions

Batch processing made turnaround time a major constraint: users often submitted work and inspected results later. Yet early computing also included interactive control, displays, and direct operation. Time sharing expanded access to interactive sessions; it did not invent all human-computer interaction. The important change was that repeated feedback became available within an ongoing task, allowing people to explore and revise their work.

Sutherland's Sketchpad demonstrated direct manipulation of represented objects. Engelbart's NLS and its 1968 demonstration combined pointing, structured documents, links, and collaboration in a system intended to augment intellectual work. These systems asked what activities the computer should support, not only how to make an existing command easier to enter.

Xerox PARC explored personal workstations, bitmapped displays, pointing, and graphical applications. The commercial Xerox Star appeared in 1981, before Apple's Lisa in 1983 and Macintosh in 1984. These products developed related ideas under different cost and market constraints. Shared conventions for selecting, copying, opening, and saving reduced how much users had to relearn between applications. A graphical interface still required training and did not make every task self-explanatory.

Card, Moran, and Newell's 1983 work connected task performance with cognitive models. GOMS described goals, operators, methods, and selection rules, allowing predictions for specified tasks and assumptions about skilled behavior. Shneiderman's interface principles and Nielsen's usability engineering provided practical evaluation methods. Their value lies in making designs inspectable and testable; neither a model nor a checklist substitutes for observing the relevant users.

Norman's work clarified conceptual models, feedback, mappings, affordances, and signifiers. An affordance is a possible action in the relation between an actor and an object; a signifier communicates where or how to act. A handle may permit pulling while a label communicates whether pulling is the intended action. This distinction helps explain why an operation can be physically possible yet difficult to discover.

The Web extended design across devices, languages, connection speeds, and independently authored pages. Touch interfaces changed target sizes, available feedback, and the visibility of gestures. Mobile use also introduced interruption and changing physical contexts. Accessibility and inclusive design made it harder to treat one familiar user, device, or sensory ability as the default for everyone.

AI-assisted interfaces add uncertainty about what a system will produce and what actions it may take. Some questions are familiar—status visibility, correction, delegation, and recovery—while model-generated errors add new forms of difficulty. A useful design identifies the evidence available to the user, when review is possible, and how an incorrect action can be corrected. Conversational fluency alone does not answer those questions.

#### Cognition, Evaluation, and Designing for Diversity

#### How Human Cognition Shapes Interface Requirements

Working-memory demands depend on the task, familiarity, grouping, and available external cues. Miller's discussion of seven items is not a rule limiting menus to seven choices, and later chunk estimates are not fixed interface capacities. Keep relevant information visible when people need it: show the previous selection, the amount being confirmed, or the steps already completed. Recognition can reduce recall demands, while a stable command language can be efficient for practiced users.

A mental model is the user's account of how a system behaves. Consider an editor that displays “Saved” immediately after a network request starts. If the request fails, the interface has taught the wrong relation between feedback and persistence. Showing saving, confirmed save, and a recoverable failure helps users predict what survives a reload. Feedback should correspond to the state that matters for the task.

Mappings connect controls to effects. Consistent labels, grouping, and spatial arrangements can make those mappings easier to learn. Signifiers make available actions apparent, but visual appearance must be backed by interaction semantics: a control should have a meaningful name and a usable keyboard behavior. More minimal visual styling is not automatically less cognitive work if it hides distinctions people need.

Pointing has measurable costs. One common Fitts's-law formulation is `T = a + b log₂(1 + D/W)`, where `D` is movement distance, `W` is target width along the movement direction, and `a,b` are fitted for the task and device. For `D=400`, increasing `W` from 20 to 80 changes the index from about 4.39 to 2.58. This predicts a direction of improvement under the model, not a universal time saving or a complete account of touchscreen use.

Separate slips from mistakes. A slip executes an unintended action despite a correct goal; a mistake follows an incorrect understanding or plan. Spacing controls, constraining invalid inputs, and preserving undo can reduce the cost of slips. Clear explanations and better task structure can address mistaken understanding. Repeated confirmation dialogs can become habitual clicks, so use confirmations where their information helps a meaningful decision and provide recovery where possible.

#### Empirical Evaluation Methods

Choose a method for the question. A formative usability study observes representative people attempting realistic tasks to discover obstacles. Think-aloud can expose an interpretation, but speaking can change behavior and timing. Interviews investigate experience and reported reasons; analytics records selected behavior. Neither automatically reveals every cause.

Small iterative studies can uncover useful problems quickly. The familiar five-user recommendation is not a coverage guarantee. Under a simple independent-discovery model, a problem found by each participant with probability `p` is found by at least one of `n` participants with probability `1−(1−p)^n`. With `p=0.31` and five participants this is about 84%; with `p=0.05` it is only about 23%. Real probabilities differ across problems, tasks, and user groups. [Nielsen's account](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-you-only-need-to-test-with-5-users/) explicitly discusses comparable users and iterative redesign.

Heuristic evaluation provides an expert inspection before or alongside user studies. Its findings are candidate problems, not measurements of how often users will fail. Test task completion, errors, recovery, and satisfaction with appropriate participants; measuring small differences in completion rates or time requires a study sized for that purpose, not automatically five people.

A randomized A/B test compares outcomes under two assigned alternatives. Define the assignment unit, primary outcome, exposure, observation period, and stopping rule. Randomization supports a causal comparison when implementation and analysis preserve it; interference between users or selective missing data can complicate interpretation. Report effect size and uncertainty, not only whether a threshold was crossed.

The chosen metric is part of the design claim. More clicks can mean engagement or confusion; fewer cancellations can mean satisfaction or an obstructed exit. Combine the metric with task outcomes, qualitative evidence, and checks for burdens on different groups. Record what changed, what evidence improved, and what remains uncertain.

#### Designing for Diversity: Accessibility and Inclusion

Accessibility concerns whether people with disabilities can perceive, understand, and operate a system. It must be evaluated in actual tasks, including assistive technologies and different input methods. WCAG organizes web requirements under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust, with conformance levels A, AA, and AAA. A technical conformance assessment has a defined version and scope; it is not a claim that every person will find every task easy.

Use semantic controls, meaningful labels, visible focus, keyboard access, appropriate alternatives for images and audio, and sufficient contrast. Test reading order and status announcements with a screen reader. A custom control that looks like a button may lack the behavior a native button already provides. ARIA can communicate semantics when used correctly, but does not implement missing keyboard behavior.

Targets also require enough space to select. [WCAG 2.2's minimum target-size criterion](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html) specifies a 24-by-24 CSS-pixel requirement with defined spacing alternatives and exceptions. This differs from a platform's recommended touch size and does not mean that the minimum is comfortable in every context.

Inclusive design also considers language, text direction, date and number formats, device capability, interruption, and connectivity. Captions or larger controls can help beyond the group they were first intended to serve, but benefits are not identical for everyone. Involve affected users, preserve meaningful choices, and test the complete workflow rather than only a page's appearance.

#### What Studying This Changes

You should be able to turn “the interface is confusing” into a testable explanation: the action was not discoverable, its consequence was mispredicted, the result was unclear, or recovery was unavailable. Each suggests a different design change.

Choose one task, such as editing a reservation. Observe users without teaching the intended route, record where their expectations differ from the system, and change one cause. Test the revised flow, including keyboard use and a failed network request. Compare actual task success and recovery, not just preference for the new appearance.

This practice connects HCI to systems correctness: the interface communicates which actions are possible, which changes persisted, and which decisions remain with the user. A reliable backend and an understandable interaction are both needed for a task to succeed.

#### Traps

| Trap | Why it misleads | Better response |
|---|---|---|
| Designing from your own familiarity | A designer knows conventions and hidden state that new users may not. | Observe realistic tasks with the intended participants. |
| Treating appearance as the whole experience | Discoverability, task structure, feedback, and recovery can fail in an attractive interface. | Specify and test the full task outcome. |
| Using five participants as a universal sample size | Discovery probability and estimation precision depend on the problem and population. | Use iterative discovery studies and size quantitative studies for their own questions. |
| Adding accessibility only at the end | Interaction structure and control semantics can already exclude users. | Design and test keyboard, screen-reader, and other relevant paths early. |
| Optimizing one business metric as if it represented user benefit | A metric can improve when users are confused or prevented from leaving. | Check task outcomes, unwanted effects, and affected groups. |
| Treating a heuristic or cognitive law as a complete explanation | Its assumptions may omit context, skill, device, or social activity. | Use it to propose a change, then test the prediction in context. |

### 6.3 — Data Engineering and Data Science

Data engineering builds the processes that collect, transform, store, and deliver data for use. Data science formulates questions, examines evidence, builds models, and evaluates conclusions. They meet at the meaning of a record: what happened, to whom, when, and under which collection procedure?

Consider a dashboard reporting completed orders. The total depends on whether retries create duplicates, refunds revise old records, time zones change the reporting day, and “completed” has the same meaning across systems. Correct SQL cannot settle an undefined business concept. A useful data product needs both a reliable computation and an explicit interpretation.

The work connects databases (§4.4), distributed processing (§4.6–4.8), statistics (§2.5), and machine learning (§5.2). Data may be transformed before or after storage, and analysis may inform changes to the collection process itself. The goal is evidence suitable for a particular decision, with its provenance and limitations available for inspection.

*Prerequisites: SQL and relational concepts (§4.4), basic algorithms (§2.6), and probability and statistics (§2.5). Begin with a small dataset whose records you can inspect before introducing distributed infrastructure.*

#### From Statistical Analysis to Reproducible Data Pipelines

Data processing has roots in censuses, commercial record keeping, scientific measurement, and statistical work before electronic computers. Tabulation already required decisions about categories, units, missing records, and checks. As the computing histories show, business data processing and scientific calculation placed different demands on storage, input, and repeated operations. Bigger machines did not remove the need to define what was being counted.

Statistical methods developed ways to separate variation from evidence about populations and interventions. Interactive computing then made repeated fitting, plotting, and exploration easier. Tukey's exploratory data analysis emphasized looking for unexpected structure and collection problems. Exploration can change the question; confirmatory analysis must account for which hypotheses and choices were selected after inspecting the data.

S and later R made statistical models, vectors, and graphics accessible in interactive environments. Python's array, plotting, tabular-data, and notebook tools connected analysis with general programming. These ecosystems reduced the effort of expressing an analysis. They did not make package defaults appropriate for every sampling process, nor did they make an executable notebook automatically reproducible.

Relational databases and data warehouses organized durable records and analytical queries. At web scale, MapReduce provided a model in which map operations emit key–value pairs and reduce operations combine grouped values, with the framework managing distributed execution and recovery. Shuffling keys between workers can dominate cost. Partitioning and reducing data before a shuffle often matter more than increasing worker count.

Spark began at Berkeley in 2009 and was open-sourced in 2010, according to its [project history](https://spark.apache.org/faq.html). Reusing distributed datasets helped iterative and interactive workloads avoid repeatedly reconstructing intermediates. Its execution still includes scheduling, shuffles, serialization, and possible disk spill; “in memory” is a design opportunity, not a promise that a workload fits in RAM or is always faster.

Event logs and stream processors made arrival order and processing delay explicit design issues. Lambda architectures maintain batch and speed paths with a serving layer; Kappa-style designs emphasize processing and replaying a log through one main path. A log by itself is neither architecture. Each choice must explain corrections, late events, historical recomputation, and the cost of maintaining consistent definitions.

Cloud warehouses, transformation tools, and orchestrators changed where computation runs and how it is managed. Versioned SQL and dependency graphs make some changes easier to test and inspect. They complement rather than replace decisions about data ownership, access, retention, and semantics. No single tool combination is required for every analytical workload.

Machine-learning pipelines added requirements such as reproducing the features available at prediction time. Feature stores and model-tracking systems help organize that work, but consistency requires more than using the same column name. A training feature computed from information that arrived after the prediction would have been made can leak future information, even when the transformation code is shared.

#### Pipelines, Quality, and the Analytics Stack

#### Data Pipelines: From Source to Sink

Specify a pipeline's sources, outputs, record identity, time semantics, and recovery behavior. Delivery can be at least once while an output is made effectively once through deduplication and atomic updates. An “exactly once” claim must state its boundary: a processor's state, a database write, and an external notification need not share the same guarantee.

Suppose events `e1:+10` and `e2:+20` are followed by a retry of `e1:+10`. Blindly adding every arrival gives 40 instead of 30. Persisting the event ID and applying its effect in one transaction can prevent that duplicate effect. Recording the ID before a non-atomic effect can instead lose work after a crash. Idempotency is about repeated effects under a specified operation and input, not merely the presence of an upsert command.

ETL transforms before loading into the destination; ELT loads first and transforms there. Choose where to validate, minimize, and transform data based on privacy requirements, source constraints, compute, and downstream use. Raw retention can aid replay, but needs controlled access and a retention policy. A reproducible recomputation identifies input versions, transformation code, and parameters.

Separate event time from processing time. An event occurring at 23:59 may arrive at 00:03, so a daily total needs a rule for late data and revision. A watermark is an estimate or policy about event-time progress, not a universally reliable statement that every earlier event has arrived. For ML features, track when information became available as well as when it describes the world.

An orchestrator schedules dependencies and retries; it does not make task side effects correct. A backfill should recompute a specified historical interval without corrupting newer results. Version guards, partition replacement, transactional publication, and explicit failure handling can help, depending on the destination. Inspect the complete retry path, including what happens after the output commits but before success is acknowledged.

#### Data Quality: Measuring and Maintaining Trust

Define quality relative to use. Completeness, freshness, validity, uniqueness, consistency, and accuracy are different properties. A field can satisfy its type and range while describing the wrong person. A table can contain no nulls while systematically excluding failed transactions. Checks need an account of which records should exist, not only rules for those that arrived.

The grain of a table specifies what one row represents. Suppose two orders have totals 100 and 60; the first has two line items and the second has one. Joining order totals to line items and summing the repeated total gives 260, although the order-level total is 160. No row is necessarily malformed. The error comes from changing the unit of observation without changing the aggregation.

Use schema checks, key and relationship checks, reconciliation against independent counts or totals, and distribution monitoring. An unusual change may be a data defect or a real event. A fixed “within 20% of last week” check requires context such as holidays or a changed product. Route invalid records and alerts to an owner with a correction process rather than silently discarding inconvenient data.

Lineage connects outputs to input versions and transformations, helping locate where a meaning or value changed. Data contracts specify expectations between producers and consumers: fields, units, identity, timing, allowed corrections, and change notification. Automatically collected lineage and declared contracts are only as complete as the covered systems. Document the definition and owner of important metrics alongside their implementation.

#### Analytical Methods: From Exploration to Causation

Exploration examines distributions, missingness, unusual records, and relationships before committing to an interpretation. Preserve the distinction between observations that suggested a hypothesis and evidence reserved to test it. Removing an outlier requires a reason about the measurement or population; an inconvenient value is not automatically an error.

Randomized experiments assign an intervention at a defined unit, such as a user or household. The resulting comparison estimates an effect for that experiment's population, exposure, and period. Randomization balances confounders in expectation, not exactly in every finite sample. Check assignment, actual exposure, missing outcomes, and interactions between units before treating a difference as a causal estimate.

Suppose 50 of 1,000 control users and 60 of 1,000 treatment users complete a task. The observed increase is 1 percentage point, or 20% relative to the control rate. With independent users, a simple normal-approximation 95% interval for the difference is roughly −1 to +3 percentage points. The relative increase alone exaggerates how much is known. Report the absolute effect, uncertainty, and what size would matter in practice.

A p-value measures incompatibility with a specified null model under the analysis assumptions; it is not the probability that the null is true or that chance caused the result. Plan sample size and stopping around the effect and precision needed. Repeatedly checking a fixed-sample significance threshold and stopping when it is crossed changes the error rate. Valid sequential designs can allow ongoing monitoring when their rules are followed.

Observational causal methods replace randomization with other assumptions. Difference-in-differences relies on a suitable parallel-trends claim; regression discontinuity uses behavior near an assignment threshold; instrumental variables require relevance and restrictions on alternative causal paths. These assumptions concern how the data arose, not just which regression was fitted. Domain knowledge, negative controls, and sensitivity analyses can assess parts of the argument without proving every untestable assumption.

Prediction, description, and intervention answer different questions. A model can predict cancellations accurately using a variable that would not reduce cancellations if changed. Keep population selection, measurement, data processing, and statistical inference visible in the final conclusion. More rows reduce some sampling uncertainty; they do not automatically repair selection bias or an invalid causal design.

#### What Studying This Changes

You should be able to state a metric's population, row grain, time window, inclusion rules, and revision policy. Trace one reported value through its transformations to the source records. If its meaning cannot be stated, a faster pipeline will not resolve the problem.

Build a small order pipeline containing duplicate deliveries, late events, corrections, and one-to-many joins. Retry after a simulated failure and reconcile the result against a manually computed reference. Then construct a feature using only information available at a specified prediction time.

For an analysis, write the question and intended decision before choosing a method. Compare effect sizes and uncertainty, and separate exploratory findings from confirmatory evidence. This joins operational reliability with statistical reasoning: the computation and the interpretation both need support.
